lessons.name: Big O Notation
lessons.desc: A language for describing how time and memory grow as input size n grows — ignoring constants and lower-order terms. The first thing an interviewer asks after you propose an algorithm.
lessons.q: Is O(2n) the same as O(n)?
lessons.qsub: Why do we ignore constants and lower-order terms? · How do you measure space complexity including recursion stack? · When is O(n log n) actually slower than O(n²) in practice?
lessons.what:
Do function, bilkul same kaam. 10 items pe dono turant jawab dete hain. 10 lakh items pe ek turant jawab deta hai aur doosra 4 minute le leta hai. Farak code ki khoobsurti mein nahi hai — farak growth mein hai.

Big O usi growth ko likhne ka tarika hai: input n badhega, to kaam kitni tezi se badhega? Ye tumhe seconds nahi batata — ye shape batata hai.

Isiliye stopwatch bekaar hai. Tumhara laptop tez hai, interviewer ka slow, server ka alag. Par O(n²) har machine pe O(n²) hi rehta hai.
lessons.analogy: Shaadi mein 100 mehmaan. Tum sabse ek-ek baar haath milao — 100 handshakes, O(n). Ab har mehmaan har doosre se mile — 4,950 handshakes. Mehmaan sirf double karo (200), handshakes 4 guna ho jaate hain. Yahi O(n²) ka dard hai.
lessons.why:
Interviewer "iski complexity kya hai?" isliye puchta hai kyunki ye ek sawaal bata deta hai ki tumne code likha hai ya socha hai. Jo bandaa apne hi solution ki cost nahi bata sakta, wo use improve bhi nahi kar sakta.

Aur asli kaam mein: wo O(n²) loop staging pe 200ms leta hai (100 rows), prod pe 30 second (50,000 rows). Code same, data alag — aur pata tabhi chalta hai jab customer chillata hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. n pehchano — input ka wo hissa jo bada ho sakta hai: array ki length, string ka size, tree ke nodes.
2. Loops aur recursive calls gino. Loop ke andar loop = guna (n × n). Ek ke baad ek loop = jod (n + n).
3. Jod mein sirf sabse bada term rakho — n² + n + 50 ban jata hai n². Kyunki n = 10,000 pe n² = 10 crore hai aur n sirf 10 hazaar — chhota term dikhta hi nahi.
4. Constants phenk do — 3n → O(n).
5. Space alag se gino: extra arrays + recursion ki depth. Ye step 90% log bhool jaate hain.
where: Array index, hash lookup · space: constant
Binary search on sorted input · space: constant
Single linear pass · space: usually constant
Merge/Quick sort, heap ops · space: O(n) for merge

qa.q: Is O(2n) the same as O(n)?
qa.a: Yes — we drop constant factors. Both describe linear growth; the constant doesn't change how the curve scales, and for large n the gap between 2n and n is negligible compared to the gap between n and n².

qa.q: What is the complexity of a while loop that halves n each iteration?
qa.a: O(log n) — each step removes half the input, so it takes log2(n) steps to reach 1. Binary search is the canonical example.

lessons.name: Arrays in JavaScript
lessons.desc: Contiguous-indexed storage with O(1) access by index. In JS, arrays are objects with length tracking — methods like push/pop/splice/slice cover most manipulation you'll need.
lessons.q: Why is unshift O(n) but push O(1)?
lessons.qsub: How do you detect if an array is sorted in O(n)? · How do you rotate an array right by k in O(1) space? · What does arr.slice() with no args return?
lessons.what:
Shelf pe numbered boxes — box 0, box 1, box 2. Box 5 chahiye? Seedha wahan haath daalo. Poori shelf dekhne ki zaroorat nahi. Yahi arr[5] hai — O(1), chahe array 10 ka ho ya 10 lakh ka.

Par ek baat log miss karte hain: JS mein array koi special native structure nahi hai. Ye ek object hai jiski keys numbers hain, aur ek length counter apne aap update hota rehta hai.

Saari cost isi se nikalti hai. End pe kaam karo (push/pop) — koi hila nahi, O(1). Shuru ya beech mein kaam karo (shift/unshift/splice) — baaki sabko ek-ek jagah khisakna padta hai, O(n).
lessons.analogy: Train ke coach mein seat number se seedha apni seat pe — O(1). Par seat 1 pe naya passenger ghusa do, to sabko ek-ek seat aage khisakna padega — O(n). Yahi unshift hai.
lessons.why:
Interviewer do cheezein dekhta hai. Pehli: kaunsa method original array badal deta hai (push, splice, sort, reverse) aur kaunsa naya array deta hai (map, filter, slice). Ye confusion production bugs ka sabse aam source hai — React state mutate kar diya to re-render hi nahi hota.

Doosri: cost. "Array ke shuru se element hatao" pe agar tum shift loop mein laga doge, wo chupke se O(n²) ban jaata hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Array banate hi engine ek object banata hai jisme index numbers hi keys hain, aur ek hidden length counter set hota hai.
2. arr[i] padhne pe engine us key ko seedha memory address se resolve karta hai — ek constant-time step.
3. push pe engine length dekh kar agle slot mein value daal deta hai aur counter badha deta hai — kuch hilta nahi.
4. Beech se splice karne pe engine baaki sab elements ek-ek position shift karta hai — isliye O(n).
5. map/filter/slice ek bilkul naya array banate hain aur original ko chhoote tak nahi.

qa.q: Why is unshift O(n) but push O(1)?
qa.a: push appends at the end, where the array has spare capacity, so it's amortized O(1). unshift inserts at index 0, forcing every element to shift right by one — O(n).

qa.q: In-place vs creating a new array — when does it matter?
qa.a: In-place avoids O(n) extra space and often lets you solve with two pointers in one pass. Problems like Rotate Array and Set Matrix Zeroes explicitly ask for in-place to test this.

lessons.name: Objects, Map, and Set
lessons.desc: Hash-based structures giving O(1) average lookups, inserts, and deletes. Map preserves insertion order and accepts any key type; Set enforces uniqueness. The single most-used tool in interviews.
lessons.q: Map vs plain Object — which do you reach for and why?
lessons.qsub: Why does checking Set.has beat indexOf on an array? · How do you build a frequency map of characters in a string? · What happens when you set a key that already exists in a Map?
lessons.what:
Phone ka contact list — naam type karo, number turant. 5 contacts ho ya 5000, same speed. Phone list scan nahi karta; naam ko ek formula (hashing) se seedha uski jagah mein badal deta hai.

Object, Map, Set — teeno isi principle pe chalte hain. Isliye insert, lookup aur delete sab average O(1).

Farak sirf itna: Object keys ko string bana deta hai. Map koi bhi key leta hai aur insertion order yaad rakhta hai. Set sirf values rakhta hai aur duplicate apne aap nikaal deta hai.
lessons.analogy: Kitaab ke aakhir wala index — "Recursion" dhoondhna hai to poori kitaab nahi palatte, index se seedha page 142 pe jaate ho. Hash function wahi index hai.
lessons.why:
Ye interview ka sabse zyada kaam aane wala tool hai. Jab bhi tumhara solution "har element ke liye baaki sab mein dhoondho" wala O(n²) ban raha ho — jawab lagbhag hamesha hash hai.

Doosra test: Map vs Object vs Set mein se sahi chuno, aur kyun chuna wo bhi bata sako.

Kaise sochein:

1. Key insert hote hi ek hash function usse ek number mein badal deta hai.
2. Wo number decide karta hai internal array mein kaunsa bucket use hoga.
3. Lookup pe wahi hash function dobara chalta hai — seedha sahi bucket mil jaata hai, poora data scan nahi hota.
4. Do keys ka hash same aa jaye (collision) to engine us bucket ke andar chhoti list bana deta hai — isliye worst case O(n) hota hai, average O(1).
5. Map ek extra linked structure rakhta hai taaki insertion order bhi yaad rahe.

qa.q: Map vs plain Object — which do you reach for and why?
qa.a: Map. It accepts any key type, preserves insertion order, has a size property, and avoids prototype-key collisions (like a key named 'constructor'). For simple string-keyed counting either works, but Map is the safer habit.

qa.q: Two Sum — why does a Map make it O(n)?
qa.a: Store each number with its index as you scan. For each x, check if target - x is already in the map — that lookup is O(1), so one pass suffices instead of a nested loop.

lessons.name: Recursion
lessons.desc: A function that calls itself with a smaller version of the same problem. Two mandatory parts: a base case that stops, and a recursive case that makes progress toward it. Backbone of trees, backtracking, and DP.
lessons.q: What is the space complexity of recursion?
lessons.qsub: What happens if a recursive function has no base case? · How deep can recursion go in JS before RangeError? · Why is naive Fibonacci exponential but memoized version O(n)?
lessons.what:
Almirah saaf karni hai jisme boxes hain, aur un boxes ke andar bhi boxes. Tum poori almirah ek saath nahi sochte — tum kehte ho "is box ko saaf karo, aur andar wale box ke liye wahi kaam dobara".

Recursion bas yahi hai: function khud ko chhote input ke saath bulata hai. Do hisse hamesha chahiye — base case (kahan rukna hai) aur recursive case (chhota kaise banana hai).

Aur ek baat jo 90% log interview mein bhool jaate hain: har call stack pe ek frame chhodti hai. Isliye recursion ka space O(1) nahi, O(depth) hota hai — chahe tumne ek bhi array na banaya ho.
lessons.analogy: Matryoshka gudiya — har gudiya ke andar chhoti gudiya. Kholte jao jab tak sabse chhoti solid gudiya na mile (base case). Phir wapas ek-ek karke band karte hue upar aao — yahi unwind hai, aur yahi tumhara answer banata hai.
lessons.why:
Trees, graphs, backtracking, DP — ye saare topics recursion ke upar khade hain. Recursion nahi aayi to Phase 4 se aage kuch nahi hoga.

Aur interview mein sabse jaldi pakda jaane wala bug yahi hai: base case missing ya galat → RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.

Kaise sochein:

1. Function call hote hi ek naya frame call stack pe chadhta hai, apne local variables ke saath.
2. Sabse pehle base case check hota hai — input already simplest form mein hai to seedha value return kar do.
3. Base case nahi mila to function khud ko chhote input ke saath phir se call karta hai.
4. Ye chain tab tak chalti hai jab tak base case na aaye — stack upar hi upar badhta jaata hai. Stack ki maximum height hi tumhara space hai.
5. Base case hit hote hi values wapas neeche aati hain, har pending call apna kaam poora karke stack se pop ho jaata hai.
where: O(depth) space · space: d is recursion depth
O(n) · space: O(h) where h = height

qa.q: What is the space complexity of recursion?
qa.a: O(depth) for the call stack, not O(1). A function recursing n deep uses O(n) stack space even if it takes no other memory. That's why deep recursion can stack overflow while an iterative loop won't.

qa.q: How do you convert recursion to iteration?
qa.a: Replace the call stack with an explicit stack (LIFO for DFS-style) or queue (for BFS-style). The iterative version uses O(1) stack memory instead of O(depth) — the reason iterative tree traversals exist.

lessons.name: The 5-Step Problem Framework
lessons.desc: A repeatable interview loop: understand → examples → brute force → optimize → code → test. Interviewers grade process as much as the final answer; this framework keeps you from freezing.
lessons.q: What should you do in the first 60 seconds of a problem?
lessons.qsub: What clarifying questions do you always ask? · How do you decide brute force is too slow? · Why should you state the brute force even when you know the optimal?
lessons.what:
Adhoori requirements wala ticket mila aur tumne seedha code likhna shuru kar diya — aadhe raaste pe pata chalega galat cheez bana rahe the. Interview mein bhi wahi hota hai.

Isliye ek fixed loop hai: samjho → examples → brute force → optimize → code + test. Har step ka apna kaam hai, aur har step tumhe agle step ka raasta deta hai.

Sabse zaroori baat: interviewer sirf final code nahi de rahe number. Wo dekh rahe hain tum uljhe hue problem ko kaise todte ho — kyunki asli kaam mein rozana wahi karna hota hai.
lessons.analogy: Doctor ke paas jaate ho to wo seedha dawai nahi likhta — pehle sawaal poochta hai (samjho), phir symptoms match karta hai (examples), phir ek aam wajah sochta hai (brute force), phir test karwa ke pakka karta hai (optimize), tab prescription likhta hai (code). Seedha dawai likhne wale doctor pe kaun bharosa karega?
lessons.why:
Interviewer ke paas 45 minute hain aur wo ek sawaal ka jawab dhoondh raha hai: "is bande ke saath kaam karna kaisa rahega?" Chup-chaap type karna uska sabse bada red flag hai.

Aur practical fayda: framework tumhe panic se bachata hai. Unfamiliar problem aaye to socha nahi jaata — par step 1 hamesha kiya jaa sakta hai. Wahi 3 minute mein dimaag khul jaata hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Samjho — problem apne words mein zor se bolo. Constraints poochho: n kitna bada, negative numbers aayenge, duplicates, empty input?
2. Examples — ek chhota input khud banao aur haath se output nikaalo. Ek edge case bhi (khaali, ek element, sab same).
3. Brute force — jo sabse seedha solution soojhe wo bolo, chahe slow ho, aur uski complexity bhi bolo. Ye tumhara safety net hai — kuch na kuch to haath mein hai.
4. Optimize — poochho "kaunsa kaam baar-baar ho raha hai?" Wahi jagah hash map, two pointer, ya sorting se katati hai. Pattern ka naam lo.
5. Code + test — ab likho. Phir apne hi example pe line-by-line trace karke dikhao, phir edge cases.
where: State it, then optimize · space: 5 min
Name the pattern + complexity · space: 5-10 min
Write + trace edge cases · space: remaining

qa.q: What should you do in the first 60 seconds of a problem?
qa.a: Restate the problem in your own words, confirm constraints (input size, negatives, empty input, duplicates), and ask a clarifying question. This anchors the problem and signals structured thinking.

qa.q: What if you're stuck after 10 minutes?
qa.a: Go back to examples — brute-force one more small case by hand. If still stuck, say what you know and what's blocking you out loud; interviewers prefer a clear 'I'm stuck because...' to silent panic.

lessons.name: Space Complexity
lessons.desc: How much extra memory your algorithm needs beyond the input, as a function of n. Counts new arrays, hash maps, and the recursion call stack. Interviewers ask it as often as time complexity.
lessons.q: What's the space complexity of a recursive tree traversal?
lessons.qsub: What does 'in-place' strictly mean? · Does slice() count as extra space? · What's the stack space of an iterative vs recursive binary search?
lessons.what:
Tumhare function ko ek room mila kaam karne ke liye. Space complexity poochti hai: tumne us room mein kitna naya saaman rakha?

Input khud nahi ginte — wo pehle se tha. Sirf wo jagah ginte hain jo tumhara solution khud banata hai: naye arrays, hash maps, aur — ye sabse zyada miss hoti hai — recursion ka call stack.

Isliye ek function jo ek bhi array na banaye par n deep recurse kare, uska space O(1) nahi O(n) hai. Har pending call stack pe apni jagah ghere baithi hai.
lessons.analogy: Tiffin le kar office aaye ho — wo tumhara input hai, wo to aana hi tha. Par khaana garam karne ke liye office ka ek extra bartan use kiya — wahi tumhara extra space hai. Aur agar 10 log line mein khade intezaar kar rahe hain apni baari ka, wo jagah bhi ghiri hui hai — yahi call stack hai.
lessons.why:
Time behtar karne ke chakkar mein log chupke se space badha dete hain — ek hash map bana diya, ek copy bana li — aur bolte reh jaate hain "solution O(1) space hai". Interviewer wahi pakadta hai.

Aur bahut si problems explicitly kehti hain "O(1) extra space mein karo" — wo line hi bata rahi hai ki two-pointer ya in-place swap wala solution chahiye, hash map nahi.

Kaise sochein:

1. Dekho function ke andar kaunse naye arrays, objects ya maps bane jo input mein nahi the.
2. Un structures ka size n ke saath kaise badhta hai — wahi unka order hai.
3. Function recursive hai? To socho ek waqt mein maximum kitni calls stack pe pending reh sakti hain — wahi depth hai. (Total calls nahi — sirf ek saath khadi calls.)
4. Dono ko jodo aur sabse bada term rakho.
5. Sirf gine-chune variables jo n ke saath nahi badhte — wo O(1) hai, chahe wo 10 variables hi kyu na ho.
where: O(n) extra · space: avoid unless asked

qa.q: What's the space complexity of a recursive tree traversal?
qa.a: O(h) where h is the tree height — the call stack holds one frame per level. For a balanced tree that's O(log n); for a degenerate (linked-list shaped) tree it's O(n).

qa.q: When would you trade time for space, or vice versa?
qa.a: Caching (memoization) trades O(n) space for O(1) time per subproblem. If the constraint forbids extra space, you accept a slower algorithm — the problem statement usually dictates the trade.

lessons.name: Fibonacci & Recursion Trees
lessons.desc: The canonical recursion lesson: fib(n) = fib(n-1) + fib(n-2) with no memoization explodes into an exponential tree that recomputes the same subproblems. Memoizing collapses it to O(n). The same tree shape underlies Climbing Stairs and House Robber.
lessons.q: Why is naive fib O(2^n) when it only recurses n levels deep?
lessons.qsub: How many nodes are in fib(5) naive vs memoized? · Why does the iterative version use only two variables? · Which problems share the exact same recurrence tree as fib?
lessons.what:
fib(5) ko todo: fib(4) + fib(3). Phir fib(4) ko todo: fib(3) + fib(2). Ruko — fib(3) do baar nikal raha hai. Aur wo dono baar poora kaam dobara karega.

Ye pattern har level pe dogunna hota hai. fib(5) mein 15 calls chalti hain, fib(30) mein 13 lakh se zyada — sab wahi purane jawab dobara-dobara nikalte hue. Yahi O(2ⁿ) hai.

Ilaaj ek line ka hai: jo ek baar nikal liya use likh lo. Wahi memoization hai, aur wahi poore Dynamic Programming ka darwaza hai.
lessons.analogy: Class mein sabse pucho "kal ka homework kya tha?" Har bacha apne do dost se poochta hai, wo apne do se… poori class ka shor. Agar ek bacha jawab board pe likh de, to baaki sab seedha padh lete hain. Board hi memo hai.
lessons.why:
Ye topic Fibonacci ke baare mein hai hi nahi. Ye overlapping subproblems pehchanne ke baare mein hai — wahi ek skill jo poora Phase 7 (DP) unlock karti hai.

Interview mein exponential solution bata ke ruk jaana half credit hai. "Yahan same subproblem repeat ho raha hai, memo laga ke O(n) kar deta hoon" — asli test yahi line hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. fib(n) apne aap ko do baar bulata hai — fib(n-1) aur fib(n-2).
2. Un dono se do-do aur calls — tree har level pe roughly double ho jaata hai.
3. Chhoti values (fib(2), fib(3)) tree ki alag-alag branches mein baar-baar aati hain.
4. Har repeat call apna poora kaam dobara karti hai, kyunki jawab kahin store nahi hua.
5. Memo lagate hi har repeat branch ek O(1) lookup ban jaati hai — tree collapse ho kar n distinct subproblems ki ek chain reh jaati hai.
6. Dhyaan do: depth hamesha n hi thi. Time branching se aata hai, space depth se.

qa.q: Why is naive fib O(2^n) when it only recurses n levels deep?
qa.a: Depth is O(n), but each node spawns TWO children, so the tree has ~2^n nodes and the same work is recomputed at every branch. Depth sets SPACE; branching factor sets TIME.

qa.q: What does memoization actually do here?
qa.a: It caches the answer for each n the first time it is computed. Every duplicate branch becomes an O(1) lookup, reducing ~2^n calls to exactly n distinct subproblems — O(n) time, O(n) space.

lessons.name: Arrays & Strings
lessons.desc: Contiguous-indexed storage with O(1) index access. The default container for most problems; mastery means knowing which JS methods mutate vs copy and their costs.
lessons.q: What's the time cost of arr.shift()?
lessons.qsub: How do you find the second largest element in one pass? · When is arr.sort() O(n log n) but still fine to use? · How do you merge two sorted arrays in place from the end?
lessons.what:
Phase 0 mein dekha tha array kaam kaise karta hai. Ab asli sawaal: kaunsa method original ko badal deta hai, aur kaunsa naya array deta hai?

Ye sirf trivia nahi hai. state.push(item) likhoge to array badal to jaayega, par uska pata (reference) wahi rahega. React pata dekhta hai, andar nahi jhaankta — usko lagega kuch badla hi nahi, aur re-render skip ho jaayega.

Bug dikhta nahi, error nahi aata — bas UI purani reh jaati hai. Isiliye ye interview mein bhi poocha jaata hai aur production mein bhi kaatta hai.
lessons.analogy: Register mein entry — purane hi page pe overwrite kar do (mutate), to bahar wale ko dekh ke pata hi nahi chalega kuch badla. Naya page likh ke upar rakh do (copy), to farak seedha dikh jaata hai. React sirf page dekhta hai, likhawat nahi.
lessons.why:
Interviewer ek line mein pata laga leta hai ki tumne React sirf use kiya hai ya samjha bhi hai. push/splice/sort/reverse badalte hain; map/filter/slice/spread naya dete hain.

DSA side pe iska doosra roop hai: in-place solutions. "O(1) extra space mein karo" ka matlab hai naya array banane ki ijaazat nahi — two pointer se hi kaam nikalna hoga.

Kaise sochein:

1. Dekho method array ka length ya order seedha badal raha hai — agar haan, wo mutating hai.
2. Method bilkul naya array return karta hai aur original waisa hi rehta hai — wo non-mutating hai.
3. React state ke liye pehle copy banao: [...arr] ya arr.slice().
4. Copy pe change karo, phir usi copy ko setState mein do — naya reference gaya, re-render hua.
5. DSA mein ulta chahiye — jahan O(1) space bola ho, wahan original ko hi two pointer se badlo.

qa.q: What's the time cost of arr.shift()?
qa.a: O(n) — every remaining element must move down one index. For a queue-like structure prefer a head-pointer index or a proper Deque implementation.

qa.q: In-place algorithms — why do interviews love them?
qa.a: They prove you can manage O(1) extra space. Problems like Rotate Array and Set Matrix Zeroes explicitly require it, and in-place techniques (two pointers, cycle sort) show up in hard problems.

lessons.name: Strings & Characters
lessons.desc: Immutable sequences of characters. In JS, string methods return NEW strings — building strings in a loop is O(n²) if done naively. Character codes and palindrome checks are the core patterns.
lessons.q: Why is string concatenation in a loop slow?
lessons.qsub: How do you check if a string is a valid palindrome ignoring non-alphanumerics? · What does charCodeAt return for emoji vs ASCII? · How do you reverse words in a sentence in place?
lessons.what:
String ek chhapi hui kitaab jaisi hai. Ek shabd badalna ho to poora naya page chhapna padta hai — purane page pe likha nahi jaa sakta. JS mein string immutable hai.

Isliye s += c dikhne mein ek chhota kaam lagta hai, par andar se: poori purani string copy karo, aakhir mein ek character jodo, naya string bana do.

Loop mein n baar karo to copy hone wali length har baar badhti hai — 1 + 2 + 3 + … + n = O(n²). Fix ek line ka hai: array mein push karo, aakhir mein ek baar join('').
lessons.analogy: Photocopy machine — ek line add karni hai to poori purani sheet dobara photocopy karo naye line ke saath. Dus line ka document banane mein tumne 55 line photocopy kar daali. Array + join matlab: saari lines alag-alag likho, aakhir mein ek baar stapler mar do.
lessons.why:
Ye classic "ek chhota change, bada farak" wala signal hai. Interviewer dekhta hai ki tum += ka chhupa hua cost pehchante ho ya nahi.

Aur strings ke baaki sawaal — anagram, palindrome, sliding window — sab isi neev pe khade hain: string ko badla nahi ja sakta, sirf padha ja sakta hai. Isliye kaam frequency map ya do pointer se hota hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. s += c pe JS ek naya string object banata hai — purani string chhui bhi nahi jaati.
2. Naya banane ke liye purani ke saare characters copy hote hain. Ye kaam string ki current length ke barabar hai.
3. Har iteration pe length badhti hai, isliye har copy pichhli se mehengi hoti hai.
4. Sab jod do: 1+2+3+…+n = n(n+1)/2 → O(n²).
5. Array mein push karo — array mutable hai, koi copy nahi hoti, har push O(1).
6. Aakhir mein join('') ek hi baar poora scan karta hai — O(n). Bas.

qa.q: Why is string concatenation in a loop slow?
qa.a: Strings are immutable. Each += allocates a brand new string copying the whole previous content — n concatenations cost O(1+2+...+n) = O(n²). Collect pieces in an array and join() once for O(n).

qa.q: Anagram detection — what's the optimal approach?
qa.a: Sort both strings and compare (O(n log n)), or build two frequency maps (O(n)). For a single string pair, the frequency-map comparison is cleanest; sort-and-compare is shorter to write.

lessons.name: Hash Map
lessons.desc: Key-value storage with O(1) average insert/lookup/delete by hashing the key. The #1 interview tool: it converts 'scan the array for something' from O(n) per check to O(1).
lessons.q: HashMap vs Array — when does each win?
lessons.qsub: How do you count frequencies of every character? · Why is 'value -> index' a Map in Two Sum but a plain array in others? · How do you build a map of anagram groups?
lessons.what:
Two Sum: array mein do number dhoondho jinka jod target ho. Seedha tarika — har number ke liye baaki poore array mein doosra dhoondho. Nested loop, O(n²).

Ab palto: har number pe poochho "mujhe target - x chahiye — kya wo pehle dikh chuka hai?" Agar dekhe hue numbers ek register mein likhte jao, to ye sawaal O(1) mein jawab de deta hai.

Bas. Poora solution ek pass, O(n). Hash map ka kaam yahi ek hai: "dhoondho" ko "yaad hai?" mein badal dena.
lessons.analogy: Shaadi mein 500 mehmaan aur tumhe apna dost dhoondhna hai. Har table pe jaake dekhna = O(n). Par entry pe ek register hai jisme sabka naam aur table number likha hai — naam bolo, table number milo. Register hi hash map hai.
lessons.why:
Ye interview ka sabse zyada return dene wala tool hai. Ek hi pattern — "pehle dekha hai kya?" — darjanon problems kholta hai.

Interviewer specifically ye dekhta hai: brute force O(n²) bolne ke baad tum khud hash map tak pahunchte ho ya hint chahiye hoti hai. Ye pattern-recognition ka test hai, memory ka nahi.

Kaise sochein:

1. Array ko ek hi baar left se right chalo.
2. Har element pe pehle poochho: jo chahiye (complement, ya pehle ka count) wo map mein hai?
3. Mil gaya → wahi answer hai, turant return.
4. Nahi mila → current element ko map mein daalo (value → index, ya value → count).
5. Agle pe badho. Poora array ek hi baar traverse hua — O(n) time, O(n) space.
6. Order zaroori hai: pehle check, phir insert. Ulta kiya to element khud ko match kar lega.

qa.q: HashMap vs Array — when does each win?
qa.a: Array wins when keys are dense integers 0..n-1 (frequency by index, cycle sort). HashMap wins for arbitrary keys — strings, objects, sparse integers — giving O(1) average access.

qa.q: What's the worst case for a hash map and why don't we worry?
qa.a: With a bad hash function or pathological inputs, everything lands in one bucket → O(n) operations. In interviews we assume a good hash → O(1) average, but knowing the caveat shows depth.

lessons.name: Singly Linked List
lessons.desc: Nodes holding a value and a next pointer, chained linearly. No O(1) index access — traversal is O(n). The superpowers are O(1) insertion/deletion at a known node and pointer tricks (fast & slow, dummy nodes).
lessons.q: Why use a dummy head node?
lessons.qsub: What's the cost of finding the k-th node? · Why can't you do arr[i] access on a linked list? · When reversing, why must you save next before rewiring cur.next?
lessons.what:
Treasure hunt — har chit pe agli chit ka pata likha hai. Pehli chit se hi shuru karna padega, kyunki 50vi chit kahan hai ye sirf 49vi bata sakti hai.

Linked list bilkul ye hai. Har node mein value hai aur next — agle node ka pata. Koi index nahi hai, isliye arr[50] jaisa jump possible hi nahi. 50vi node chahiye? 50 baar next follow karo — O(n).

Badla mein ek superpower milti hai: agar node ka reference tumhare paas already hai, to uske baad insert karna ya use hatana sirf do pointer badalne ka kaam hai — O(1). Array mein wahi kaam O(n) shifting maangta hai.
lessons.analogy: Treasure hunt ki chits — beech ki chit seedha nahi khol sakte, ek-ek karke aage badhna padega. Par agar chit haath mein hai, to uske baad nayi chit ghusa dena bahut aasaan hai: sirf do jagah ka pata badalna hai, baaki poori hunt waise ki waise.
lessons.why:
Interviewer array vs linked list ka tradeoff test karta hai: array random access jeetta hai, linked list known-node insert/delete jeetti hai.

Aur isse bhi zyada — pointer manipulation ka test hai. Reverse, cycle detect, merge — in sab mein ek galat order mein pointer badla to poori list tut jaati hai. Interviewer dekhta hai tum next save karna yaad rakhte ho ya nahi.

Kaise sochein:

1. head pehle node ki taraf ishara karta hai. Uske alawa list ka koi doosra darwaza nahi hai.
2. Kisi bhi node tak jaane ke liye head se next follow karte jao.
3. Insert: naye node ka next pehle set karo, phir pichhle node ka next naye pe. Ulta kiya to aage ki poori list kho gayi.
4. Delete: pichhle node ka next seedha aage wale pe point kara do — beech wala apne aap list se bahar.
5. Reverse: teen pointer — prev, cur, next. Har step pe next pehle bacha lo, tab cur.next = prev karo.

qa.q: Why use a dummy head node?
qa.a: It eliminates special-casing the head: you never write 'if this is the first node'. Operations like insertion before head, or building a result list, all start from a dummy and return dummy.next — less branching, fewer bugs.

qa.q: How does the fast & slow pointer detect a cycle?
qa.a: Two pointers move at speed 1 and 2. If there's a cycle the fast pointer laps the slow one and they meet — O(n) time, O(1) space. Same idea finds the middle node (fast reaches end, slow is at middle).

lessons.name: Stack
lessons.desc: LIFO (last-in, first-out). Push/pop/peek all O(1). Used wherever the most recent thing matters: matching brackets, undo, function calls, monotonic-pattern groundwork, parsing.
lessons.q: What's the difference between a Stack and a Queue?
lessons.qsub: What does a stack's depth represent in bracket matching? · How do you evaluate Reverse Polish Notation with a stack? · When should you use a stack vs recursion for DFS?
lessons.what:
Plates ka dher. Jo sabse aakhir mein upar rakhi, wahi sabse pehle uthegi. Beech se koi plate seedha nikalti hi nahi. Isko LIFO kehte hain — Last In, First Out.

Push aur pop dono ek hi sire pe hote hain, isliye kuch khisakna nahi padta — dono O(1).

Aur ye koi alag cheez nahi hai — JS ka call stack yahi hai. Jo function aakhir mein call hua, wahi pehle return karta hai. Recursion samajh liya matlab stack samajh liya, aur ulta bhi.
lessons.analogy: Dhaba mein dhoye hue plates ka dher — upar wali hi uthegi. Ya browser ka back button: jo page aakhir mein khola, back dabane pe wahi pehle wapas aayega. "Sabse recent cheez" jahan chahiye, wahan stack hai.
lessons.why:
Stack ek signal hai. Problem mein nesting dikhe — brackets, tags, expressions — ya "pichhla wala" chahiye ho, to jawab lagbhag hamesha stack hai.

Aur ye Phase 1 ka sabse zyada aage tak jaane wala topic hai: monotonic stack, iterative DFS, expression parsing, undo — sab isi ek structure pe khade hain.

Kaise sochein:

1. Naya element hamesha top pe jaata hai — push.
2. Nikalta bhi hamesha top se hi hai — pop. Neeche wale chhue tak nahi jaate.
3. peek sirf top dekhta hai, hataata nahi — JS mein arr[arr.length-1].
4. Dono kaam ek hi sire pe, isliye koi shifting nahi — O(1).
5. Bracket matching: opening aaya to push. Closing aaya to pop karke check karo ki wo sahi jodi ka tha. Aakhir mein stack khaali hona chahiye — kuch bacha to koi bracket band hi nahi hua.

qa.q: What's the difference between a Stack and a Queue?
qa.a: Stack is LIFO — the newest element is removed first (think stack of plates). Queue is FIFO — the oldest is removed first (think ticket line). That single property decides which fits the problem.

qa.q: How would you implement a queue using two stacks?
qa.a: Use one stack for push (inbox). On pop, if the outbox is empty, dump all of inbox into outbox (reversing order), then pop from outbox. Amortized O(1) per operation.

lessons.name: Queue
lessons.desc: FIFO (first-in, first-out). Enqueue/dequeue O(1). The engine behind BFS — level-order tree traversal and shortest-path-on-unweighted-graph exploration. In JS, a plain array works but shift() is O(n); use a head index or a real queue.
lessons.q: Why does BFS give the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
lessons.qsub: How does BFS prevent infinite loops on graphs? · In level-order traversal, why snapshot the queue size? · What changes if edges are weighted? (→ Dijkstra)
lessons.what:
Ration ki line. Jo pehle aaya, wahi pehle nikla. Beech se koi cutting nahi kar sakta. Isko FIFO kehte hain — First In, First Out.

Stack se ulta hai: stack mein dono kaam ek sire pe hote the, queue mein do alag sire hain — peeche se andar (enqueue), aage se bahar (dequeue). Isliye dono O(1).

Aur ye sirf ek data structure nahi hai — ye BFS ka poora engine hai. Ek level ke saare nodes pehle nikalte hain, tabhi agla level shuru hota hai. Wo guarantee queue hi deta hai, aur wahi guarantee unweighted graph pe shortest path banati hai.
lessons.analogy: Ration shop ki line — pehle aaya, pehle gaya. Aur BFS aise socho jaise talaab mein patthar phenka: lehrein gol-gol, ek-ek ring karke phailti hain. Pehle 1 kadam ki doori waale sab, phir 2 kadam waale. Isiliye jo pehli baar mila, wahi sabse nazdeek hai.
lessons.why:
Queue samjhe bina BFS nahi hoga, aur BFS bina Phase 4 (trees) aur Phase 5 (graphs) ka aadha hissa nahi hoga. Level-order traversal, shortest path, rotting oranges, word ladder — sab yahin se.

Aur JS-specific ek trap hai jo interviewer khaas dekhta hai: arr.shift() O(n) hai. Use BFS loop mein laga diya to poora algorithm chupke se O(n²) ho jaata hai — answer sahi aayega, par bade input pe TLE.

Kaise sochein:

1. Naya element hamesha rear (peeche) jud'ta hai — enqueue.
2. Nikalta hamesha front (aage) se hai — dequeue.
3. Do alag sire hain, isliye kuch khisakna nahi padta — dono O(1).
4. BFS mein: node nikalo, uske saare unvisited padosi peeche daal do.
5. Level-order chahiye? Loop shuru karne se pehle size = queue.length naap lo, aur utne hi nikalo. Warna current level ke saath agla level bhi mix ho jaayega.
6. Graph pe visited set zaroori hai — warna cycle mein queue kabhi khaali hi nahi hogi.

qa.q: Why does BFS give the shortest path in an unweighted graph?
qa.a: Because it explores level by level — all nodes at distance d are processed before any at distance d+1. The first time a node is reached, it's reached by a shortest route. DFS has no such guarantee.

qa.q: Why is arr.shift() bad for a queue?
qa.a: shift() reindexes every remaining element — O(n) per dequeue, O(n²) total for n operations. A head-pointer index (or linked list) makes dequeue O(1).

lessons.name: Hash Set
lessons.desc: An unordered collection of unique values with O(1) add/remove/check. Whenever a problem says 'distinct', 'unique', or 'have I seen this', a Set is the tool — cleaner than a Map of booleans.
lessons.q: Set vs Map — when do you use each?
lessons.qsub: How do you find the intersection of two arrays with O(n)? · When does a Set become worse than sorting? · How do Sets dedupe objects (identity vs equality)?
lessons.what:
Set wahi hai jo Map hai — bas value hai, key-value nahi. Sirf ek sawaal ka jawab deta hai: "ye cheez andar hai ya nahi?" — O(1) mein.

Array mein wahi sawaal includes() se poochte ho, aur wo har element check karta hai — O(n). Loop ke andar likh diya to chupke se O(n²).

Ek bonus muft mein: duplicate apne aap gayab. [...new Set(arr)] — ek line, O(n), aur order bhi bana rehta hai.
lessons.analogy: Club ke bahar bouncer ke paas guest list. Naam bolo, wo seedha uss page pe jaata hai — poori list nahi padhta. Aur list mein ek naam do baar ho hi nahi sakta — dobara likhne ki koshish karo to kuch hota hi nahi.
lessons.why:
Interviewer ek cheez dekhta hai: jab problem mein "distinct", "unique", "pehle dekha hai kya" ya "visited" aaye — tumhare dimaag mein turant Set aana chahiye.

Ye ek pattern-recognition test hai, syntax ka nahi. Map jab chahiye jab tumhe value ke saath kuch aur bhi yaad rakhna ho (index, count). Sirf "hai ya nahi" — to Set saaf hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Value add karte hi ek hash function usse ek number mein badalta hai.
2. Wo number internal array ka slot tay karta hai.
3. Value us slot mein rakh di jaati hai. Do values ka hash same aa gaya (collision) to us slot mein ek chhoti list ban jaati hai.
4. has(x) pe wahi hash dobara chalta hai — seedha slot pe. Poora set scan nahi hota.
5. Add karte waqt bhi pehle yahi check hota hai — isliye duplicate apne aap reject ho jaata hai.
6. Isliye add, has, delete — teeno average O(1), worst case O(n).

qa.q: Set vs Map — when do you use each?
qa.a: Set when you only need membership (do I have this? is it distinct?). Map when each value carries associated data (count, index). A Set is a Map without values — no lookup key for the count.

qa.q: Contains Duplicate — Set or sort?
qa.a: Set: one pass, if set.has(x) return true, else add — O(n) time O(n) space. Sorting is O(n log n) with O(1) space; for small arrays both fine, but the Set answer is the one expected.

lessons.name: Doubly Linked List
lessons.desc: Like a singly list, plus a prev pointer on every node. The prev pointer enables O(1) deletion of a node you already have — no need to find its predecessor. This is what makes LRU Cache possible.
lessons.q: Why can a doubly linked list delete a known node in O(1) but a singly one can't?
lessons.qsub: Why do LRU implementations use sentinel head/tail nodes? · When is a doubly list worse than a singly list? · What breaks if you forget to fix both prev and next links?
lessons.what:
Singly list mein ek kami hai. Node ka reference haath mein hai aur usko delete karna hai — par delete karne ke liye pichhle node ka next badalna padta hai, aur peeche jaane ka koi raasta hi nahi. Head se dobara chalo — O(n).

Doubly list ek line mein ye theek kar deti hai: har node ke paas prev bhi hai. Ab pichhla node haath mein hai, isliye delete sirf do pointer badalne ka kaam hai — O(1).

Yahi ek baat LRU Cache ko possible banati hai: hash map se node turant milta hai, aur prev ki wajah se usko list mein aage khisakna bhi O(1) hai.
lessons.analogy: Local train mein log ek doosre ka haath pakde khade hain — dono taraf se, aage wale ka aur peeche wale ka. Beech wala utarna chahe to dono padosi seedha ek doosre ka haath pakad lete hain. Kisi ko darwaze se ginti karke aana hi nahi padta.
lessons.why:
Ye topic ek hi design question ke liye hai, par wo question bahut poocha jaata hai: LRU Cache. Uska poora trick yahi hai — Map se node dhoondho O(1) mein, aur DLL se usko head pe le jaao O(1) mein.

Interviewer ye bhi dekhta hai ki tumhe cost pata hai: har node pe ek extra pointer ka memory, aur har operation mein dono taraf ke link theek karne ka discipline.

Kaise sochein:

1. Har node teen cheezein rakhta hai — value, next, aur prev.
2. Insert karte waqt chaar pointer set hote hain: naye node ke dono, aur dono padosiyon ka ek-ek.
3. Delete karte waqt do: node.prev.next = node.next aur node.next.prev = node.prev. Traversal ki zaroorat hi nahi.
4. Sentinel (dummy) head aur tail rakh lo — phir koi bhi asli node ke prev/next kabhi null nahi honge, aur saare if (node === head) wale checks gayab.
5. Node ko "aage khisakana" ek kaam nahi, do hain: pehle unlink, phir insert. Order galat kiya to list tut jaati hai.

qa.q: Why can a doubly linked list delete a known node in O(1) but a singly one can't?
qa.a: Deletion needs the predecessor to rewire its next pointer. A doubly list reaches it directly via node.prev. A singly list must traverse from the head to find it — O(n).

qa.q: How does LRU Cache combine a Map and a DLL?
qa.a: The Map gives O(1) lookup by key; the DLL tracks recency order so the least-recently-used node is at the tail. On get/put you move the node to the head; eviction removes the tail — every operation O(1).

lessons.name: Circular Linked List
lessons.desc: A linked list whose tail points back to the head, forming a loop. Common in round-robin scheduling, Josephus-style problems, and as the mental model for cycle detection.
lessons.q: How does Floyd's algorithm find the entry point of a cycle?
lessons.qsub: Why must fast advance two steps but never more? · What happens if the cycle is the whole list? · How do you safely iterate a circular list without an infinite loop?
lessons.what:
Normal list ka aakhri node null pe khatam hota hai. Circular list mein wo aakhri node wapas head ko point karta hai. Bas itna hi farak — aur poora behaviour badal jaata hai.

Ab list ka koi end hi nahi hai. Traversal apne aap ghoomta rehta hai, aur "aakhri ke baad pehla" wala kaam muft mein ho jaata hai — koi % length nahi lagana padta.

Iska doosra roop zyada important hai: agar list mein galti se aisa loop ban jaaye, to plain while (cur) kabhi rukega hi nahi. Isi ko pakadne ke liye Floyd ka slow-fast trick hai.
lessons.analogy: Antakshari — aakhri banda gaake wapas pehle ko baari de deta hai. Koi "last person" hai hi nahi. Aur cycle pakadne ka trick: gol track pe do daudne wale. Ek dheere, ek dugna tez. Track gol hai to tez wala ek na ek din dheere wale ko lap maar ke pakad hi lega. Track seedha hota to kabhi na milte.
lessons.why:
Interviewer do cheezein dekhta hai. Pehli: tumhe pata hai stopping condition chahiye, warna infinite loop — aur ye galti bahut aam hai.

Doosri, aur badi: Floyd's algorithm kyun kaam karta hai. Sirf code ratna kaafi nahi. Jawab ye hai: ring ke andar dono ho jaayein to unke beech ki doori har step pe theek 1 ghatti hai, isliye milna guaranteed hai. Fast 3 kadam le to ye guarantee tut sakti hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Aakhri node ka next null ki jagah head pe set kar do — ring ban gaya.
2. Traverse karne ke liye do { ... } while (cur !== head) — ek poora chakkar, phir ruk jao. while (cur) yahan kabhi nahi rukega.
3. Cycle pakadne ke liye slow 1 kadam, fast 2 kadam chalao.
4. Ring nahi hai to fast pehle null pe pahunch jaayega — cycle nahi.
5. Ring hai to dono andar aa jaayenge, aur unke beech ka gap har step 1 ghatega — milna pakka.
6. Cycle ka shuru chahiye? Milne ke baad slow ko wapas head pe rakho, ab dono 1-1 kadam chalao — jahan milenge wahi entry hai.

qa.q: How does Floyd's algorithm find the entry point of a cycle?
qa.a: After slow and fast meet inside the cycle, reset slow to head. Then advance both one step at a time — the math shows they meet exactly at the cycle's start. Total O(n) time, O(1) space.

qa.q: What's the difference between a circular list and a list with a cycle?
qa.a: A true circular list deliberately points the tail at the head — traversal is well-defined. A 'cycle' bug is usually unintended. The detection algorithm is identical, but a circular list is a design, not a defect.

lessons.name: Monotonic Stack
lessons.desc: A stack that always stays sorted (increasing or decreasing) by values — you pop elements that violate the order before pushing. Every element is pushed and popped at most once, so it's O(n) and solves 'next greater / next smaller' problems elegantly.
lessons.q: Why is a monotonic stack O(n) even though there's a nested while?
lessons.qsub: How do you get the previous greater element instead of next? · What changes for next smaller? · How does Largest Rectangle in Histogram use a monotonic stack?
lessons.what:
Har element ke liye uske daayein taraf ka pehla bada element chahiye. Seedha tarika: har element se aage scan karo — O(n²).

Ab palto. Jab koi naya bada element aata hai, wo ek saath kai purane elements ka jawab ban jaata hai — un sabka jo abhi tak apne bade ka intezaar kar rahe the.

To un "intezaar kar rahe" elements ko ek stack mein rakho, hamesha ghatte hue order mein. Naya element aaya — jo bhi usse chhote hain, unka jawab mil gaya, pop kar do. Har element ek baar push, ek baar pop — poora kaam O(n).
lessons.analogy: Line mein log height ke hisaab se khade hain, sabse aage sabse lamba. Peeche se ek aur lamba banda aata hai — usse chhote saare log ab uske peeche chhup gaye. Un sabka jawab "mera pehla lamba banda kaun" ek saath settle ho gaya, aur wo line se hat gaye.
lessons.why:
Ye Phase 1 ka sabse "algorithm jaisa" topic hai. Interviewer ek hi cheez dekhta hai: kya tum amortized soch sakte ho.

Code mein for ke andar while dikhta hai — pehli nazar mein O(n²) lagta hai. Par har element poore run mein zyada se zyada ek baar push aur ek baar pop hota hai, isliye total kaam 2n hai — O(n). Ye samjha ke bol dena hi asli answer hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Stack mein indices rakho, values nahi — distance nikalne ke liye index chahiye hota hai.
2. Har naye element pe: jab tak stack ka top invariant tod raha ho, use pop karo.
3. Jo element pop hua — uska jawab yahi current element hai. Jawab pop ke waqt likho, push ke waqt nahi.
4. Ab current index ko push kar do.
5. Aakhir mein stack mein jo bache — unka koi jawab tha hi nahi (default 0 / -1).
6. Direction yaad rakhne ka tarika: next greater chahiye → stack ghatta hua rakho. Next smaller chahiye → badhta hua.

qa.q: Why is a monotonic stack O(n) even though there's a nested while?
qa.a: Each element is pushed exactly once and popped at most once across the whole run. The inner while only runs across total pops = n, so the algorithm is O(n) amortized — no element is processed twice.

qa.q: Should the stack store values or indices?
qa.a: Indices. Values alone lose the distance information (Daily Temperatures needs days = i - idx) and can't handle duplicate values cleanly. Store indices and read the value via the array.

lessons.name: Deque (Double-Ended Queue)
lessons.desc: A queue that supports O(1) push/pop at BOTH ends. The workhorse for sliding-window maximum/minimum problems, where candidates must be added at the back and expired at the front.
lessons.q: Why is Sliding Window Maximum O(n) and not O(nk)?
lessons.qsub: What invariant does the deque maintain for window maximum? · How would you get the minimum instead? · Why compare nums[dq[last]] <= nums[i] with <= (not <)?
lessons.what:
Deque = queue jisme dono sire khule hain. Aage se bhi daal sakte ho aur nikal sakte ho, peeche se bhi. Chaaron kaam O(1).

Zaroorat kyun padti hai? Sliding Window Maximum socho. Window aage khiskti hai, to front se purana index bahar phenkna hai (window se nikal gaya), aur back se chhote values phenkne hain (naye bade element ke saamne wo kabhi max ban hi nahi sakte).

Do alag sire, do alag wajah. Isiliye simple queue kaafi nahi — deque chahiye. Andar rakhe elements hamesha ghatte hue order mein rehte hain, isliye front hamesha window ka maximum hota hai.
lessons.analogy: Rassa-kashi ki line dekhne wale — aage wale purane log jaate rehte hain (window aage khisak gayi), aur peeche se koi lamba aa jaaye to usse chhote log pointless ho jaate hain (unka number kabhi nahi aayega). Line ke aage hamesha sabse lamba khada rehta hai.
lessons.why:
Interviewer Sliding Window Maximum poochta hai kyunki naive solution O(n·k) hai aur deque wala O(n). Farak samajhna hi test hai.

Aur JS-specific trap: dq.shift() O(n) hai. Algorithm sahi likh ke bhi tum O(n·k) pe wapas aa sakte ho — ye bolna ki "asli deque ya head index chahiye" alag se points deta hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Deque mein indices rakho, values nahi — window expiry index se hi pata chalti hai.
2. Naya element i aaya: back se un sab ko pop karo jinki value nums[i] se choti ya barabar hai — wo ab kabhi max nahi ban sakte.
3. Ab i ko back pe push karo.
4. Front dekho: agar wahan ka index window se bahar nikal gaya (<= i - k), use hata do.
5. Window poori ban gayi (i >= k-1) to nums[front] hi is window ka maximum hai.
6. Har index ek baar andar, ek baar bahar — poora kaam O(n), monotonic stack jaisa hi.

qa.q: Why is Sliding Window Maximum O(n) and not O(nk)?
qa.a: Each index enters the deque once and leaves once. The inner while only pops total n times across the run. The window maximum is always at the front — O(1) to read. No element is ever rescanned.

qa.q: Why use a deque instead of a max-heap here?
qa.a: A heap answers max in O(log k) but can't cheaply evict the element leaving the window. The deque keeps candidates in decreasing order, evicts expired indices from the front in O(1), and reads max from the front in O(1).

lessons.name: 2D Matrix Traversal
lessons.desc: Arrays of arrays as grids. Patterns: row/column iteration, diagonal walks, spiral order, and in-place transforms (rotate, transpose, zero-out) — heavy favorites at Google/Meta.
lessons.q: How do you rotate a matrix 90° in place with O(1) space?
lessons.qsub: How do you zero out rows/columns with O(1) extra space? · What are the edge cases for spiral on a single row or column? · How do you check neighbors without index errors?
lessons.what:
2D matrix asal mein array of arrays hai. matrix[r][c] se koi bhi cell O(1) mein mil jaata hai. Wahan tak sab aasaan hai.

Dikkat traversal ke pattern mein hai. Row-by-row seedha hai. Par spiral? Diagonal? 90° rotate bina extra array ke? Yahan poora kaam index ke hisaab ka ho jaata hai.

Do trick 80% matrix problems khol deti hain: rotate = transpose + har row reverse, aur spiral = chaar boundary jo har chakkar ke baad simat'ti hain.
lessons.analogy: Chess board. Ek square batana aasaan hai (row, column). Par "bahar wale ghere se andar ki taraf gol-gol chalo" — ab tumhe chaar kinaare yaad rakhne padenge, aur har chakkar ke baad chaaron ko ek kadam andar khiskana padega.
lessons.why:
Rotate Image, Spiral Matrix, Set Matrix Zeroes — Google aur Meta ke favourite hain. Kyunki inme algorithm nahi, index ka anushasan test hota hai. Bounds check ek jagah bhool gaye to code crash karta hai.

Aur ye Phase 5 (graphs) ki neev hai: grid pe BFS/DFS matlab har cell ek node hai aur uske 4 padosi hain. Wahi dirs array jo yahan seekhoge, wahan sau baar kaam aayega.

Kaise sochein:

1. m = matrix.length (rows), n = matrix[0].length (cols). Rectangular maano, square nahi — ye pehli galti hai.
2. Rotate 90°: pehle transpose ([i][j] ka [j][i] se swap, sirf j > i ke liye — warna do baar swap ho ke wapas wahi aa jaayega). Phir har row reverse. Bas.
3. Spiral: chaar variable — top, bottom, left, right. Ek chakkar: daayein → neeche → baayein → upar. Har taraf ke baad us boundary ko ek kadam andar karo.
4. Spiral mein aakhri single row ya column double count ho jaati hai — isliye baayein aur upar wale steps se pehle top <= bottom / left <= right dobara check karo.
5. Padosi: dirs = [[1,0],[-1,0],[0,1],[0,-1]]. Har padosi pe pehle bounds check, tabhi cell padho.

qa.q: How do you rotate a matrix 90° in place with O(1) space?
qa.a: Two mechanical steps: transpose (swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i]) then reverse each row. 90° counter-clockwise is reverse each row first, then transpose. No new matrix needed.

qa.q: Spiral traversal — what's the cleanest loop structure?
qa.a: Track four boundaries (top/bottom/left/right). Walk right, down, left, up, shrinking a boundary after each full pass, and stop when boundaries cross. It's four simple loops inside one while.

lessons.name: Static vs Dynamic Arrays
lessons.desc: How arrays actually live in memory. A static array has a fixed capacity allocated once; a dynamic array (ArrayList in Java, vector in C++, every JS array) grows by allocating a bigger block and copying. Understanding the doubling strategy explains why append is O(1) amortized.
lessons.q: Why is push on a dynamic array O(1) even though resizes copy everything?
lessons.qsub: How do you insert at index 0 of an array? What is the cost? · Why would you ever prefer a static array over a dynamic one? · How many times does an element get copied over n appends?
lessons.what:
C ka array static hai — banate waqt size bata do, bas. Bhar gaya to bhar gaya.

JS ka array dynamic hai. Jagah khatam hui to engine chupchap ek dugni badi jagah leta hai, saare purane elements copy karta hai, aur tab naya element daalta hai. Tumhe pata bhi nahi chalta.

To phir push ko O(1) kaise bolte hain, jab kabhi-kabhi wo O(n) copy karta hai? Kyunki resize har baar dugni doori pe aata hai. n push ka total copy ~2n hai — per push do kadam. Isi ko amortized O(1) kehte hain.
lessons.analogy: Almirah bhar gayi. Tum ek dugni badi almirah mangwate ho aur saare kapde shift karte ho — us din poora afternoon lag gaya. Par uske baad kaafi din tak kapda rakhna ek second ka kaam hai. Aur agli baar shifting aur bhi der se aayegi, kyunki almirah dugni ho chuki hai. Rozana ka average nikaalo to shifting dikhti hi nahi.
lessons.why:
Ye ek vocabulary ka sawaal hai. "push O(1) hai" bolna aadha jawab hai. "O(1) amortized, worst case O(n) jab resize hota hai" — ye poora jawab hai.

Aur ye Phase 0 wali amortized soch ka doosra roop hai. Hash map ka resize, stack ka growth — sab isi ek idea pe chalte hain. Ek baar samajh liya to teeno jagah kaam aata hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Array do cheezein rakhta hai — size (kitne elements hain) aur capacity (kitne aa sakte hain). Ye alag hain.
2. push pe pehle dekho size < capacity hai? Haan → seedha rakh do, O(1).
3. Nahi → capacity × 2 ka naya block lo, saare purane elements copy karo — ye O(n) hai.
4. Resize kab-kab hota hai: size 1, 2, 4, 8, 16… — har baar doori dugni.
5. n push mein total copy: 1+2+4+…+n ≈ 2n. Per push baanto → ~2 kadam → O(1) amortized.
6. Doubling isliye, +1 nahi: +1 karte to har push resize karta aur total O(n²) ho jaata.

qa.q: Why is push on a dynamic array O(1) even though resizes copy everything?
qa.a: Amortization: the sum of all copy costs over n pushes is less than 2n (each element is copied only when the array doubles, at most log n times). Total work O(n), average O(1).

qa.q: What is the space overhead of a dynamic array?
qa.a: Capacity is always at least size, and often up to 2x. That is O(n) extra slack worst case — the price for amortized O(1) append.

lessons.name: Hash Table Implementation
lessons.desc: A hash table maps keys to values using an array of buckets and a hash function. Collisions are handled by chaining (linked list per bucket) or open addressing (probe for the next free slot). Hash quality decides whether lookups are O(1) or degrade to O(n).
lessons.q: How do you handle two keys hashing to the same bucket?
lessons.qsub: What makes a good hash function for a HashMap? · Compare chaining vs open addressing. · Why is a JS object lookup not always O(1)? · When does a hash table degrade to O(n)?
lessons.what:
Ab tak Map aur Set use kiye. Ab andar kholte hain — kyunki interviewer "HashMap khud banao" bhi poochta hai.

Andar sirf ek array of buckets hai. Key aayi → hash function use ek number banata hai → % buckets.length se bucket index milta hai → wahin value rakh di.

Poora khel do cheezon ka hai. Collision — do keys ek hi bucket mein aa jaayein, to kya karein. Aur load factor — kitna bhar jaane pe buckets dugne kar dein. Hash kharab hua to saari keys ek bucket mein, aur O(1) gir ke O(n) ho jaata hai.
lessons.analogy: Post office ke pin-code wale khaane. Pin-code se seedha pata chal jaata hai chitthi kis khaane mein daalni hai — saari chitthiyan padhni nahi padti. Do chitthi ek hi pin-code ki? Us khaane mein dono rakh do (chaining) — ab us khaane ki chhoti dher padhni padegi. Aur khaane bharne lagein to dugne khaane banwa lo.
lessons.why:
Do wajah. Pehli: "Design a HashMap" seedha ek interview question hai (LeetCode 706).

Doosri, aur badi: ab tak tum O(1) average bol rahe the. Interviewer poochta hai "average kyun, hamesha kyun nahi?" — jawab collision aur load factor hi hai. Ye samjha dena junior aur senior ka farak hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Ek array banao — maano 16 buckets.
2. Hash: key ko ek number mein badlo. String ke liye har character ka code jodo/mix karo, phir % buckets.length — bucket index mil gaya.
3. Collision (chaining): bucket mein ek chhoti list rakho. Nayi entry usme push, lookup pe us chhoti list mein hi dhoondho.
4. Collision (open addressing): ya phir bucket bhara ho to agla khaali slot dhoondho. Memory kam, par delete karna ulajh jaata hai.
5. Load factor: entries ÷ buckets. ~0.75 cross hua to buckets dugne karo aur saari keys dobara hash karo (rehash) — kyunki % ka jawab badal gaya.
6. Achha hash = keys sab buckets mein barabar bikhri. Kharab hash = sab ek bucket mein = O(n).
where: O(1) avg / O(n) worst · space: O(1)
O(1) avg / O(n) worst · space: O(1)
O(1) avg / O(n) worst · space: O(1)

qa.q: How do you handle two keys hashing to the same bucket?
qa.a: Separate chaining: each bucket is a linked list (or tree). Open addressing: probe linearly (or quadratically) to the next empty slot. Chaining is simpler and what most textbook maps use.

qa.q: Why does the load factor matter?
qa.a: It is the ratio of keys to buckets. Above ~0.75 the average chain length grows and lookups slow down, so the table resizes (rehash) — costing O(n) but only rarely, so amortized O(1).

lessons.name: Linear Search
lessons.desc: Scan every element until the target is found — O(n). Simple and correct, it's the baseline you improve from. Its real interview value is recognizing when a linear scan is all you need (arrays are usually small or unsorted).
lessons.q: When is linear search the right answer?
lessons.qsub: What structure does an array need for binary search to work? · Why is a single pass the lower bound for unsorted search? · How would you find the second-largest in one pass?
lessons.what:
Ek-ek karke sab dekho, jab tak mil na jaaye. Bas. Ye Phase 2 ka sabse aasaan algorithm hai — aur isiliye log iski asli baat miss kar dete hain.

Asli baat ye hai: agar array unsorted hai, to O(n) se tez kuch ho hi nahi sakta. Jawab aakhri box mein ho sakta hai, aur ye tumhe pehle se pata nahi. To har box khoolna hi padega.

Ye algorithm ki kamzori nahi — ye ek lower bound hai. Aur yahi wo baseline hai jisse aage ka har algorithm compare hota hai.
lessons.analogy: Almirah mein kapde bina kisi order ke pade hain. Apni shirt dhoondhni hai — ek-ek uthana hi padega. Ab socho: pehle poori almirah tarike se lagao, phir shirt turant milegi. Par sirf ek shirt ke liye almirah lagana — ulta mehenga pad gaya. Roz nikalni hai? Tab lagana faayde ka.
lessons.why:
Interviewer ye nahi dekh raha ki tum for loop likh sakte ho. Wo dekh raha hai ki tum judgement le sakte ho ya nahi.

Aur ek chhupa hua trap hai jo bahut log mein jaate hain: unsorted array pe binary search laga dena. Ye crash nahi karta — bas chup-chaap galat jawab deta hai. "Array sorted hai kya?" — ye clarifying question interview mein points deta hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Index 0 se shuru karo, aakhir tak chalo.
2. Har element ko target se compare karo. Mil gaya → turant return i.
3. Loop khatam ho gaya aur mila nahi → return -1. Ye "nahi mila" wala case bhoolna sabse aam galti hai.
4. Ek hi pass mein aur bhi kaam ho sakta hai — min, max, count, ya doosra sabse bada. Alag-alag loop mat likho, ek hi mein sab track karo.
5. Faisla: ek hi baar dhoondhna hai → linear. Baar-baar dhoondhna hai → ek baar sort/hash bana lo, phir har search sasta.

qa.q: When is linear search the right answer?
qa.a: When the input is unsorted and you need a single pass anyway (min/max, counting) — O(n) is optimal because you must inspect every element. The interview skill is knowing binary search doesn't apply without structure.

qa.q: Can you do better than O(n) to find a max in an unsorted array?
qa.a: No — the max could be anywhere, so every element must be inspected. That's an information-theoretic lower bound, not a weakness of the algorithm.

lessons.name: Binary Search
lessons.desc: Repeatedly halve a sorted search space: check the middle, eliminate the half that can't contain the answer. O(log n) time, O(1) space. Variants: basic search, lower/upper bound, and search on an answer space ('minimize the maximum').
lessons.q: What does 'binary search on the answer' mean?
lessons.qsub: How do you find the first and last position of a target? · How do you search a rotated sorted array? · Why must the feasibility function be monotonic for answer-space search?
lessons.what:
Sorted data ka sabse bada faayda: beech ka element dekh kar tum aadha data ek jhatke mein phenk sakte ho. Beech wala target se chhota hai? To uske baayein ka poora hissa bekaar. Gaya.

Har step pe aadha khatam — n → n/2 → n/4 → … → 1. 10 lakh elements sirf 20 steps mein. Yahi O(log n) hai.

Par asli baat ye hai: binary search sirf arrays ke liye nahi hai. Jahan bhi monotonic cheez ho — ek baar sach hua to aage hamesha sach — wahan binary search lag sakta hai. Isi ko "answer pe binary search" kehte hain, aur wahi interview mein aata hai.
lessons.analogy: Dictionary mein shabd dhoondhna — beech ka page kholo, dekho tumhara shabd pehle aata hai ya baad mein, aadhi dictionary side mein. Koi dictionary shuru se nahi padhta. Aur yaad rakho: ye tabhi kaam karta hai kyunki dictionary sorted hai. Shabd bikhre hue hote to beech ka page kuch batata hi nahi.
lessons.why:
Binary search ka basic version har koi likh leta hai. Interview mein variants aate hain, aur wahin log phaste hain — pehla occurrence, aakhri occurrence, insertion position, rotated array.

Aur sabse bada level: answer pe binary search. Problem mein sorted array hai hi nahi — "kam se kam speed kya honi chahiye taaki kaam h ghante mein ho jaaye?" Yahan tum jawab ki range pe binary search karte ho. Ye pehchanna hi asli test hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. lo = 0, hi = n - 1. Beech nikalo: mid = lo + ((hi - lo) >> 1).
2. arr[mid] target hai? Mil gaya.
3. Chhota hai? To target daayein hi ho sakta hai → lo = mid + 1.
4. Bada hai? Target baayein → hi = mid - 1.
5. lo > hi ho gaya → hai hi nahi, -1.
6. Answer pe search: array ki jagah jawab ki range [lo, hi] lo. Ek feasible(x) function banao jo O(n) mein bataye "x se kaam ho jaayega?". Wo function monotonic hona chahiye — ek baar true, aage hamesha true. Bas, wahi binary search hai.
where: O(log R) × O(n) check · space: O(1)

qa.q: What does 'binary search on the answer' mean?
qa.a: Instead of searching an array, search the space of possible ANSWER values. For 'minimum speed to eat all bananas in h hours', speeds range 1..max; binary search that range, and each check simulates eating in O(n). Feasibility must be monotonic (if speed works, any higher speed works).

qa.q: When does while (l <= r) fail?
qa.a: l <= r with l=mid+1/r=mid-1 works for exact search but can infinite-loop or miss boundaries for lower-bound problems. For first/last occurrence, the cleaner pattern is while (l < r) with r = mid, converging to a single index.

lessons.name: Merge Sort
lessons.desc: Divide & conquer sort: split in half, sort each half recursively, then merge two sorted halves in O(n). Guaranteed O(n log n), stable, but needs O(n) extra space. The merge step is a reusable interview pattern.
lessons.q: Why is merge sort always O(n log n) while quick sort isn't?
lessons.qsub: What makes merge sort stable? · How does the merge step count inversions? · Why does merge sort need O(n) space?
lessons.what:
Do pehle se sorted list ko jodna aasaan hai — dono ke saamne wale element compare karo, jo chhota hai use uthao. Ek pass, O(n).

Merge sort is baat ko ulta chalata hai: array ko aadha-aadha todo, jab tak ek-ek element na bach jaaye (ek element apne aap sorted hai). Phir upar aate hue har jodi ko merge karte jao.

Split hamesha theek beech se hota hai, isliye depth hamesha log n — quick sort ki tarah kabhi bigadta nahi. Guarantee O(n log n). Keemat: O(n) extra jagah.
lessons.analogy: Do teachers ne apni-apni answer sheets marks ke hisaab se laga li. Ab ek combined list banani hai — dono dher ke upar wale compare karo, jo chhota hai wo naye dher mein. Dobara. Dobara. Kisi ko poora dher dobara nahi dekhna padta — kyunki dono pehle se lage hue hain.
lessons.why:
"Sort likh ke dikhao" pe merge sort sabse safe jawab hai — worst case bhi O(n log n), aur stable hai.

Par asli wajah merge step hai. Wo akela step alag se kaam aata hai: do sorted list jodna, inversions ginna, linked list sort karna, external sort (data RAM mein aata hi nahi). Merge sort yaad rakhne se zyada zaroori hai merge yaad rakhna.

Kaise sochein:

1. Array ki lambai 1 (ya 0) hai? Wo already sorted hai — wapas de do. Base case.
2. Beech se do hisso mein todo.
3. Dono hisso ko recursively sort karo. (Ispe bharosa rakho — haath se trace mat karo.)
4. Merge: do pointer, dono list ke shuru pe. Chhota wala uthao, uska pointer aage.
5. Ek list khatam? Doosri ka bacha hua hissa seedha jod do — wo already sorted hai.
6. Stability ke liye <= use karo, < nahi — barabar hone pe baayein wala pehle. Yahi ek chinh stable aur unstable ka farak hai.
where: O(n log n) · space: O(n) extra
O(n log n) · space: O(log n) stack

qa.q: Why is merge sort always O(n log n) while quick sort isn't?
qa.a: Merge sort always splits exactly in half, so depth is always log n and each level costs O(n). Quick sort's pivot can land badly — on already-sorted input it degenerates to O(n²). Merge trades guaranteed time for O(n) space.

qa.q: Why is merge sort good for linked lists?
qa.a: Linked lists have no O(1) random access, so array-sort strategies like indexing and quicksort's partitioning are awkward. Merge sort only needs to walk and rewire pointers — O(n log n) with O(log n) stack space.

lessons.name: Quick Sort
lessons.desc: Pick a pivot, partition the array so smaller elements sit left and larger right, then recurse on both sides. O(n log n) average, in-place, no extra space — but worst case O(n²) on sorted input with a bad pivot choice.
lessons.q: Quick sort vs merge sort — which do you choose and when?
lessons.qsub: Why is quick sort not stable? · What does the partition step leave behind that Quick Select reuses? · How much stack space does recursion cost in the worst case?
lessons.what:
Ek element ko pivot chun lo. Ab array ko is tarah ghumao ki: pivot se chhote saare baayein, bade saare daayein.

Ab ek baat notice karo — pivot apni final sorted jagah pe pahunch chuka hai. Use dobara chhoona hi nahi. Ab wahi kaam baayein aur daayein hisse pe alag-alag repeat karo.

Merge sort se ulta hai: merge sort ka kaam jodne mein hai, quick sort ka todne mein. Isliye quick sort ko merge wala extra array chahiye hi nahi — sab kuch in-place. Par pivot galat chun liya to O(n²).
lessons.analogy: Class ko height ke hisaab se line mein lagana. Ek bachhe ko reference bana do — usse chhote uske baayein, bade daayein. Ab wo bachha apni sahi jagah pe khada hai, use bhool jao. Ab dono groups mein alag-alag yahi karo. Par agar tumne har baar sabse chhote bachhe ko reference banaya — to har round mein sirf ek sahi jagah pahuncha, aur kaam n round le gaya.
lessons.why:
Do cheezein test hoti hain. Pehli: pivot ka chunaav. Already-sorted array pe pehla element pivot banaya to har partition bilkul unbalanced — O(n²). Middle ya random pivot lo. Ye jawab interviewer sunna chahta hai.

Doosri, aur zyada kaam ki: partition step khud ek algorithm hai. Quick Select aur Dutch National Flag — agle do topics — poore isi ek step pe khade hain. Quick sort bhool bhi jao, partition mat bhoolna.

Kaise sochein:

1. Ek pivot chuno — beech wala ya random. Pehla/aakhri fixed mat lo.
2. Do pointer: i baayein se, j daayein se.
3. i ko aage badhao jab tak koi element pivot se bada (ya barabar) na mile. j ko peeche laao jab tak koi chhota na mile.
4. Dono ruk gaye aur i <= j → swap karo, dono ek kadam aur.
5. i > j hote hi array do hisso mein bat chuka hai. Dono pe recursion.
6. Balanced partition → depth log n → O(n log n). Har baar ek taraf khaali → depth n → O(n²).
where: O(n log n) · space: O(log n) stack

qa.q: Quick sort vs merge sort — which do you choose and when?
qa.a: Quick sort for in-place O(1) space with average O(n log n) — great for arrays. Merge sort when you need guaranteed O(n log n), stability, or linked lists. If worst-case guarantees matter, merge sort; if memory is tight, quick sort.

qa.q: How do you avoid quick sort's O(n²) worst case?
qa.a: Choose a good pivot — middle element, or median-of-three. A fixed first/last pivot on already-sorted input causes the worst case. Randomizing or taking the middle keeps partitions balanced in practice.

lessons.name: Kadane's Algorithm
lessons.desc: Find the maximum-sum contiguous subarray in one pass: at each element, decide whether to EXTEND the current subarray or START a new one. O(n) time, O(1) space. Behind Maximum Subarray and its circular variant.
lessons.q: What is the ONE decision Kadane's makes per element?
lessons.qsub: How do you extend Kadane's to return the subarray itself? · How does the circular variant handle all-negative arrays? · Why does best start at -Infinity?
lessons.what:
Mahine ka profit-loss record hai. Wo continuous stretch dhoondhna hai jiska total sabse zyada ho.

Brute force: saare stretches try karo — O(n²). Kadane ek hi sawaal pe sab kaat deta hai. Har din pe sirf ek faisla: pichhle stretch ko aage badhaun, ya yahin se naya shuru karun?

Aur jawab hamesha ek line ka hai: agar pichhla total negative ho chuka hai, to usse chipke rehna sirf tumhara aane wala profit kam karega. Chhod do, naya shuru karo. Bas — ek pass, O(n), ek variable.
lessons.analogy: Kharche ka register. Pichhle hafte ka hisaab −5,000 pe hai. Aaj 2,000 kamaye. Purane hisaab mein jodoge to −3,000. Naya hisaab shuru karo to +2,000. Jo bojha tumhe neeche kheench raha hai, use dhona band karo.
lessons.why:
Ye DP ka sabse chhota version hai — poori table ki jagah sirf ek number yaad rakhna. Yahi soch Phase 7 mein baar-baar chahiye hogi.

Aur interview mein iska ek chhupa hua trap hai jo bahut log pakde jaate hain: best = 0 se shuru kar dena. Saare numbers negative hon ([-3, -1, -7]) to jawab 0 aa jaayega — par khaali subarray allowed hi nahi tha. Sahi jawab -1 hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Do variable: cur (abhi chal raha stretch ka total) aur best (ab tak ka sabse achha).
2. Har element x pe ek faisla: cur = max(x, cur + x).
3. x jeeta → naya stretch yahan se shuru (purana bojha tha). cur + x jeeta → purana stretch aage badha.
4. Phir best = max(best, cur). Ye alag se rakhna zaroori hai — cur baad mein gir sakta hai, par best yaad rakhta hai.
5. best ko -Infinity se shuru karo, 0 se nahi.
6. Indices bhi chahiye? Jab x jeete tab start = i note kar lo, aur jab best update ho tab [start, i] save kar lo.

qa.q: What is the ONE decision Kadane's makes per element?
qa.a: Whether to extend the current subarray (cur + x) or start a new one at x (cur = x). We extend only when it improves the sum; otherwise the new element starts fresh. The best answer seen is tracked along the way.

qa.q: Why does Kadane's work but brute force is O(n²)?
qa.a: The key insight is optimal substructure — the best subarray ending at i is either just nums[i] or nums[i] plus the best subarray ending at i-1. That single recurrence collapses all O(n²) candidate subarrays into O(n) states.

lessons.name: Boyer-Moore Voting
lessons.desc: Find the majority element (appears more than n/2 times) in O(n) time and O(1) space. Maintain a candidate and a counter: matching votes increment, non-matching decrement, and when the counter hits zero, adopt the current element. A favorite at Meta.
lessons.q: Why does Boyer-Moore work?
lessons.qsub: Why can't a non-majority element win the voting? · How do you extend it to n/3? · Why is this better than a frequency map here?
lessons.what:
Ek array mein koi element aadhe se zyada baar aata hai. Use dhoondhna hai — O(n) time aur O(1) space mein. Hash map allowed nahi (wo O(n) space hai).

Trick constraint mein hi chhupi hai. "Aadhe se zyada" ka matlab: agar majority ka har vote kisi doosre vote se cancel kar do, to bhi majority ke kuch vote bach jaayenge. Baaki sab poora khatam ho jaayenge.

To bas yahi karo: ek candidate aur ek count. Match → +1. Mismatch → −1. Count 0 hua → naya candidate. Aakhir mein jo bacha, wahi majority hai.
lessons.analogy: Rassa-kashi. Har vote ek taraf khinchta hai, aur do vipreet vote ek doosre ko kaat dete hain. Agar ek team ke paas aadhe se zyada log hain, to saare cancel ho jaane ke baad bhi us team ka koi na koi khada hi rahega. Rassa unhi ki taraf.
lessons.why:
Frequency map se ye problem 30 second mein ho jaati hai — O(n) time, par O(n) space. Interviewer wahi bolta hai jo asli sawaal hai: "O(1) space mein kar sakte ho?"

Ye test karta hai ki tum constraint ko hathiyaar bana sakte ho ya nahi. "> n/2" sirf ek shart nahi hai — wahi poore algorithm ki jaan hai. Ye pehchanna hi asli answer hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. candidate = null, count = 0.
2. Har element x pe: count === 0 hai? To candidate = x. (Purana candidate poori tarah cancel ho chuka.)
3. x === candidate → count++. Warna count--.
4. Bas. Aakhir mein candidate hi majority hai.
5. Kyun kaam karta hai: har count-- asal mein ek majority vote ko ek non-majority vote se cancel karna hai. Non-majority ke paas aadhe se kam vote hain, isliye wo majority ko poora kaat hi nahi sakte.
6. Majority ki guarantee nahi hai? To ek doosra pass chala ke candidate ki ginti confirm karo.

qa.q: Why does Boyer-Moore work?
qa.a: Pair up each occurrence of the majority element with a non-majority element; there are more majority elements than all others combined, so after all cancellations something survives — and it must be the majority. The counter is just bookkeeping for the pairing.

qa.q: Does it need a verification pass?
qa.a: If the problem guarantees a majority exists, no. If not, the candidate could be wrong — count it and confirm it exceeds n/2. Safe interview practice is to verify even when the guarantee exists.

lessons.name: Quick Select
lessons.desc: Find the k-th smallest/largest element without fully sorting: run the partition step, and only recurse into the side that contains the target index. O(n) average, O(1) extra space, O(n²) worst case.
lessons.q: Why is Quick Select O(n) average instead of O(n log n)?
lessons.qsub: What's the target index for k-th smallest vs k-th largest? · How does partition order guarantee the left side is all smaller? · Why doesn't the worst case show up on random data?
lessons.what:
k-va sabse bada chahiye. Sabse seedha: poora sort karo, index utha lo — O(n log n). Par tumne poori list rank kar di jabki sirf ek rank chahiye tha.

Quick Select wahi partition step use karta hai jo Quick Sort ka hai. Partition ke baad pivot apni final jagah pe hota hai — maano p. Ab teen mein se ek baat sach hai:

p === k → mil gaya. p < k → jawab daayein hai. p > k → baayein. Har baar sirf ek taraf jaate ho, doosri poori phenk dete ho. Isliye n + n/2 + n/4 + … = 2n — O(n) average.
lessons.analogy: Race khatam. Sirf ye jaanna hai ki 5va kaun aaya. Poori list rank karna bekaar hai. Ek runner ko reference banao, sabko us se aage/peeche baant do — ab uski rank pakki hai. 5 usse aage hai? To sirf aage wale group mein dekho, peeche wale bhool jao.
lessons.why:
Interviewer "kth largest" isliye poochta hai kyunki iske teen jawab hain, aur teeno alag-alag situation mein sahi hain:

Sort + index — O(n log n), sabse simple. Min-heap size k — O(n log k), streaming ke liye best. Quick Select — O(n) average, par input mutate karta hai aur worst case O(n²). Teeno bol dena aur kab kaunsa bata dena — wahi poora answer hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. k-va sabse bada chahiye? Us index pe badlo: target = n - k. (k-va sabse chhota → target = k - 1.) Ye conversion sabse aam galti hai.
2. lo se hi tak partition chalao — wahi Lomuto jo quick sort mein tha.
3. Partition ne pivot ki final jagah p lauta di.
4. p === target → nums[target] hi jawab hai. Ruk jao.
5. p < target → lo = p + 1. Warna hi = p - 1. Sirf ek taraf.
6. Worst case se bachne ke liye pivot random chuno — warna sorted input pe O(n²).

qa.q: Why is Quick Select O(n) average instead of O(n log n)?
qa.a: Because we recurse into only ONE side, not both. The work is n + n/2 + n/4 + ... which converges to 2n. It's O(n²) worst case when every pivot is extreme — same risk as quick sort.

qa.q: Quick Select vs a heap for k-th largest — which when?
qa.a: Heap is O(n log k) and reads the top k in order. Quick Select is O(n) average for just the one answer, but mutates the array and doesn't preserve order. If you need the sorted top-k, heap; if only the k-th value, quick select.

lessons.name: Dutch National Flag
lessons.desc: Sort an array of three distinct values (like 0s, 1s, 2s) in one pass with O(1) space using three pointers. It's the three-way partition technique powering Sort Colors.
lessons.q: Why don't you advance mid after swapping with hi?
lessons.qsub: What's the exact invariant at the start and end of each iteration? · How would this generalize to k colors? · Why is it called the 'Dutch national flag'?
lessons.what:
Array mein sirf teen tarah ki values hain — 0, 1, 2. Sort karni hai, ek hi pass mein aur bina extra jagah ke.

Teen pointer teen zone banate hain. lo ke baayein sab 0 pakke ho chuke. hi ke daayein sab 2 pakke ho chuke. mid beech mein chalta rehta hai — aur uske aur lo ke beech sab 1 hain.

Ek hi galti hai jo sab karte hain: hi ke saath swap ke baad mid ko aage mat badhao. Jo cheez daayein se aayi hai, wo abhi tak dekhi hi nahi gayi.
lessons.analogy: Laundry teen basket mein — safed baayein, rangeen beech, kaale daayein. Tum beech se kapde uthate ho. Safed mila → baayein phenko, aage badho. Rangeen → wahin chhodo, aage badho. Kaala → daayein phenko — par jo kapda daayein se badle mein aaya, use abhi dekha hi nahi. Aage mat badho, pehle usko dekho.
lessons.why:
Ye Quick Sort ke partition ka three-way version hai — aur wo tab kaam aata hai jab array mein duplicates bahut hon. Normal two-way partition duplicates pe bekaar ho jaata hai; three-way sab barabar wale ek saath nikaal deta hai.

Aur interview mein iska ek bahut specific test hai: counting sort (do pass — gino, phir likho) bhi O(n) hai. Interviewer bolega "ek hi pass mein karo". Tabhi DNF chahiye.

Kaise sochein:

1. lo = 0, mid = 0, hi = n - 1.
2. Invariant yaad rakho: [0, lo) sab 0 · [lo, mid) sab 1 · (hi, n) sab 2 · [mid, hi] abhi dekha nahi.
3. nums[mid] === 0 → lo ke saath swap, dono lo++ aur mid++. (Jo lo se aaya wo 1 hi tha — already dekha hua.)
4. nums[mid] === 1 → sahi jagah pe hai. Sirf mid++.
5. nums[mid] === 2 → hi ke saath swap, hi--, aur mid ko chhod do. Naya element abhi dekha nahi gaya.
6. mid > hi hote hi khatam. Ek pass, O(n), O(1) space.

qa.q: Why don't you advance mid after swapping with hi?
qa.a: The value swapped in from hi is unexamined — it could be a 0 that belongs at lo. So the loop re-checks it at the same mid index. Swaps with lo DO advance mid because the value swapped in was just checked (it was a 1, or was already < mid).

qa.q: When is three-way partitioning better than counting and rewriting?
qa.a: Counting 0s/1s/2s and rewriting is also O(n) but needs a second pass. Dutch National Flag is one pass in place — required when the problem forbids extra arrays or counts, and it generalizes the two-pointer pattern.

lessons.name: Insertion Sort
lessons.desc: Build the sorted array one element at a time: take each element and insert it into the already-sorted prefix, shifting larger elements right. O(n^2) worst but O(n) on nearly-sorted input — and stable, in-place, and the fastest sort for tiny arrays.
lessons.q: When is insertion sort actually the right choice?
lessons.qsub: What happens on an already-sorted array? How many shifts? · Why does the best case run in O(n)? · How does shifting differ from swapping?
lessons.what:
Taash khel rahe ho. Naya card uthaya — haath mein jo cards hain wo pehle se lage hue hain. Tum naye card ko uski jagah pe ghusa dete ho, bade cards ko thoda right khisaka ke. Poora haath dobara nahi lagate.

Yahi insertion sort hai. Array ka ek prefix hamesha sorted maano, aur har naye element ko us prefix mein uski sahi jagah pe daal do.

Iski asli khaasiyat: ye adaptive hai. Data already lagbhag sorted hai to koi shift karna hi nahi padta — O(n). Merge aur quick sort us case mein bhi poora O(n log n) kaam karte hain.
lessons.analogy: Taash ka haath. Naya card aaya — tum use dekhte ho aur seedha sahi jagah pe daal dete ho, bade cards ko thoda khisaka ke. Aur agar cards already lage hue aa rahe hain, to har card seedha aakhir mein chala jaata hai — koi mehnat hi nahi.
lessons.why:
Interviewer O(n²) sort implement karne ko nahi bolega. Wo ye dekhta hai ki tumhe pata hai algorithm ka chunaav input ki shakal pe depend karta hai.
