Aur ek asli baat: asli sorting libraries isi pe khadi hain. Timsort (Python, Java, V8) chhote runs pe insertion sort chalati hai, phir merge karti hai. Introsort (C++) bhi chhote hisso pe insertion sort pe switch karti hai. Kyunki chhote n pe O(n log n) ke constants O(n²) se mehenge pad jaate hain.

Kaise sochein:

1. i = 1 se shuru. Maano [0, i) already sorted hai (ek element wala prefix to hamesha sorted hai).
2. cur = arr[i] ko ek variable mein bacha lo — kyunki uski jagah pe likha jaayega.
3. j = i - 1 se peeche chalo. Jab tak arr[j] > cur, us element ko ek jagah right shift karo: arr[j+1] = arr[j].
4. Ruk gaye? Jo gap bacha hai wahi cur ki jagah hai — arr[j+1] = cur.
5. Dhyaan do: ye shifting hai, swapping nahi. Shift mein ek write hoti hai, swap mein teen. Isliye ye tez hai.
6. > use karo, >= nahi — barabar pe ruk jaana hi stability deta hai.

qa.q: When is insertion sort actually the right choice?
qa.a: Nearly-sorted data: each element shifts only a little, so the inner loop is O(1) on average and the whole thing is O(n). Also tiny arrays (n < ~15) where O(n^2) beats the recursion and allocation overhead of merge/quick.

qa.q: Why is it stable?
qa.a: The inner loop only shifts elements that are STRICTLY greater than cur (arr[j] > cur). Equal elements are never moved past each other, so original relative order is preserved.

lessons.name: Bucket Sort
lessons.desc: Distribute elements into k ordered buckets by value range, sort each bucket (often with insertion sort), then concatenate in order. O(n + k) average when values spread uniformly; degenerates to O(n^2) when they all land in one bucket.
lessons.q: Why is average case O(n + k)?
lessons.qsub: How do you pick the bucket index formula? · What is the space overhead if k = n? · Why does uniform distribution matter so much?
lessons.what:
Ek baat pakki maani jaati hai: comparison se sort karne pe O(n log n) se tez ho hi nahi sakta. Ye theorem hai.

Bucket sort us hadd ko todta hai — kyunki wo compare karta hi nahi. Wo values ki range ka faayda uthata hai: har value dekh ke seedha bata deta hai wo kis bucket mein jaayegi.

Teen kadam: scatter (range ke hisaab se baanto) → sort (har bucket chhota hai, insertion sort kaafi) → gather (buckets ko order mein jod do). Shart ek hi hai: data barabar bikhra hona chahiye. Sab ek bucket mein aa gaye to O(n²).
lessons.analogy: Post office. Chitthiyan pehle pincode range ke hisaab se alag-alag bori mein daali jaati hain — koi tulna nahi, seedha pincode padha aur bori mein daal di. Phir har bori ke andar ki chitthiyan alag se lagayi jaati hain. Boriyon ka order hi asli sorting hai — aakhir mein bas jod do.
lessons.why:
Ye topic ek conceptual sawaal ke liye hai: "O(n log n) se tez sort possible hai?" Jawab: comparison-based mein nahi. Par agar tum values ke range/distribution ke baare mein kuch jaante ho, to haan.

Aur wahi soch counting sort aur radix sort mein bhi hai. Interview mein iska sabse aam roop: "frequency ke hisaab se top K" — wahan frequency (0 se n tak) hi bucket index ban jaati hai, aur poora kaam O(n) ho jaata hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. min aur max nikalo, aur tay karo kitne buckets (k) chahiye. Aksar k = n lete hain.
2. Scatter: har value ka bucket index nikalo — ((x - min) / (max - min)) × k, phir floor.
3. Sabse badi value ka index theek k aa jaata hai — out of range. Math.min(k - 1, idx) se clamp karo.
4. Sort: har bucket alag se sort karo. Buckets chhote hain, isliye insertion sort hi best hai.
5. Gather: buckets ko 0 se k-1 tak jod do. Bas — poora array sorted.
6. Uniform distribution → har bucket mein ~1 element → O(n + k). Sab ek bucket mein → ek hi O(n²) insertion sort → sab bekaar.

qa.q: Why is average case O(n + k)?
qa.a: Scattering and gathering each touch every element once (O(n)). If the distribution is uniform, each bucket holds ~n/k elements, and insertion-sorting them costs O((n/k)^2) per bucket — k buckets total O(k·(n/k)^2) = O(n²/k), which for k ≈ n is O(n).

qa.q: When does it degenerate to O(n^2)?
qa.a: When the distribution is NOT uniform — e.g. all values pile into one bucket. That bucket now contains n elements and insertion sort on it is O(n²). Bucket sort is only fast for known well-spread distributions.

lessons.name: Binary Search on a Range
lessons.desc: The lower-bound/upper-bound form of binary search: find the FIRST index where the predicate becomes true (or the first element >= target). Unlocks first/last occurrence, insertion position, and counting occurrences — problems where plain 'find target' binary search is not enough.
lessons.q: Why hi = mid instead of hi = mid - 1 here?
lessons.qsub: Why does hi start at arr.length (not length-1)? · What does lowerBound return when the target is absent? · How do you adapt this for a peak or rotated array?
lessons.what:
Normal binary search ek value dhoondhta hai. Ye version ek seema dhoondhta hai — wo pehli jagah jahan koi condition false se true ho jaati hai.

Poora topic ek line mein: array ko values ki jagah F F F F T T T T ki tarah dekho. Tumhe pehla T chahiye. Bas.

Ye zyada taakatvar hai kyunki duplicates hone pe bhi kaam karta hai (pehla ya aakhri occurrence), aur kyunki wo "condition" kuch bhi ho sakti hai — "kya x speed se kaam h ghante mein ho jaayega?" Yahi answer pe binary search hai.
lessons.analogy: Building ki lift. Neeche ke floors pe network nahi aata, upar ke floors pe aata hai — aur ek baar aa gaya to upar hamesha aata hai. Tumhe wo pehla floor dhoondhna hai jahan se network shuru hota hai. Har floor pe rukna zaroori nahi — beech ke floor pe jao, check karo, aadhi building chhod do.
lessons.why:
Ye "binary search on the answer" family ka base hai — aur wahi family FAANG interviews mein sabse zyada aati hai.

Problem tumhe sorted array degi hi nahi. Wo bolegi: "kam se kam kitni speed chahiye taaki kaam h ghante mein ho?" Tumhe khud pehchanna hai ki jawab ki range pe ek monotonic yes/no condition hai — aur wo pehchan hi asli answer hai. Iske baad code 8 line ka hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. lo = 0, hi = n — n, n-1 nahi. Kyunki jawab "aakhir mein daalo" bhi ho sakta hai.
2. while (lo < hi) — <= nahi. Ye template converge karta hai, match pe exit nahi karta.
3. mid par condition check karo.
4. Condition false hai (arr[mid] < target) → jawab aage → lo = mid + 1.
5. Condition true hai → mid khud jawab ho sakta hai → hi = mid. mid - 1 nahi — warna jawab hi phenk doge.
6. Loop khatam → lo === hi → wahi seema hai. Return lo.

qa.q: Why hi = mid instead of hi = mid - 1 here?
qa.a: We are converging to a BOUNDARY, not pinning a match. When arr[mid] >= target, mid could itself be the first such index, so discarding it with mid-1 can skip the answer. Keeping mid lets the range shrink to exactly the boundary.

qa.q: How does this find first AND last occurrence?
qa.a: lowerBound finds the first index with value >= target. To find the last occurrence, compute the first index > target and step back one. The gap between the two bounds is exactly the count of target.

lessons.name: String Matching (KMP / Rabin-Karp)
lessons.desc: Finding a pattern in a text. Naive scanning is O(n*m); KMP precomputes a prefix function so the text pointer never backtracks (O(n+m)); Rabin-Karp uses a rolling hash to compare in O(1) per window. Know both: KMP for worst-case guarantees, Rabin-Karp for multiple patterns.
lessons.q: Why is KMP O(n+m) when naive is O(n*m)?
lessons.qsub: What does the lps array store, conceptually? · Why does Rabin-Karp use modulo arithmetic? · What is the worst case for Rabin-Karp and when does it hit it? · How would you find all occurrences of a pattern in a text?
lessons.what:
Lambi text mein ek pattern dhoondhna hai. Seedha tarika: har position se match karke dekho. Mismatch hua? Text mein ek kadam aage jao aur poora phir se — O(n×m).

Bekaar kaam yahi hai: mismatch se pehle jo characters match ho chuke the, unhe tum dobara compare kar rahe ho.

KMP ye kaam bacha leta hai. Wo pehle pattern ka apna homework karta hai — lps table — jo batati hai ki mismatch pe pattern ko kitna peeche le jaana hai. Text ka pointer kabhi peeche nahi jaata. Isliye O(n + m).

Rabin-Karp bilkul alag raasta leta hai: har window ka ek rolling hash rakho. Hash na mile → skip, O(1). Hash mil jaaye → tabhi characters compare karo.
lessons.analogy:
KMP: gaana gaate hue beech mein line galat lag gayi — tum poora gaana shuru se nahi gaate. Tumhe pata hai lyrics ka kitna hissa already match tha, wahin se aage.
Rabin-Karp: har page ka ek chhota summary code bana lo. Code na mile to page kholo hi mat. Code mil jaaye, tabhi poora page padho.
lessons.why:
Ye topic do fundamentally alag tarike dikhata hai ek hi problem ko tez karne ke: pattern ko pehle process karna (KMP) aur hashing (Rabin-Karp).

Practically: interview mein strStr aa jaaye to indexOf bolna kaafi nahi. KMP ka idea samjha dena — "text pointer kabhi backtrack nahi karta" — poora code likhe bina bhi points deta hai. Aur Rabin-Karp tab better hai jab kai patterns ek saath dhoondhne hon, ya duplicate substrings nikaalne hon.

Kaise sochein:

1. lps table: har position i ke liye — pattern[0..i] ka sabse lamba hissa jo prefix bhi hai aur suffix bhi. "ABAB" ke liye lps[3] = 2, kyunki "AB" dono taraf hai.
2. Table banane ka tarika: pattern ko khud se hi match karo — wahi loop, i aage, j mismatch pe lps[j-1] pe kood jaata hai.
3. Scan: text pe i chalao, pattern pe j.
4. Match → dono aage. Mismatch → j = lps[j-1] — i ko haath mat lagao.
5. j === m → pattern mil gaya, index i - m + 1.
6. Rabin-Karp: pehle window ka hash nikalo. Aage badhne pe puraana character ghatao, naya jodo — O(1). Hash match hua? Tab bhi characters compare karo — do alag string ka hash same ho sakta hai.

qa.q: Why is KMP O(n+m) when naive is O(n*m)?
qa.a: The lps table tells KMP exactly how far back to shift on a mismatch, so the text pointer never resets. Naive restarts from the next text position on every mismatch, revisiting characters O(n*m) times.

qa.q: When is Rabin-Karp the better choice?
qa.a: When searching for many patterns at once (like detecting duplicate code or searching a corpus), because you can keep one rolling hash and test every pattern hash in O(1). Its weakness is hash collisions, fixed with re-checking.

lessons.name: Two Pointers
lessons.desc: Two indices scan the array from the ends (or different speeds) to replace an O(n²) nested loop with one O(n) pass. The two ends of the array 'meet in the middle', exploiting the sorted structure.
lessons.q: When can two pointers replace a nested loop?
lessons.qsub: How do you avoid duplicate triples in 3Sum? · When do you use fast/slow pointers instead of left/right? · Does two pointers require the array to be sorted?
lessons.what:
Sorted array hai. Do number dhoondhne hain jinka jod target ke barabar ho. Pehla idea: har number ke saath baaki sab check karo — nested loop, O(n²).

Par ruko — array sorted hai. Usme ek information chhupi hai jo tum barbaad kar rahe ho.

Do pointer lagao — ek shuru se, ek aakhir se. Sum zyada hai? Right ko andar laao (bada number hatao). Kam hai? Left ko aage badhao. Har step pe search space ek kam hota hai, isliye poora array ek hi pass mein — O(n), aur extra space bilkul nahi.
lessons.analogy: Socho ek local train ke do darwaazon pe do checker khade hain — ek sabse aage wale coach se peeche aa raha hai, doosra sabse peeche wale coach se aage aa raha hai; beech mein milte hain, aur poori train check ho jaati hai bina kisi ek checker ko poori train dobara ghoomne diye.
lessons.why:
Interviewer ye isliye puchta hai kyunki ye pattern batata hai ki tum brute force se aage sochte ho ya nahi — kya tum extra information (sorted order, monotonic property) spot kar sakte ho aur usse ek poora loop bacha sakte ho. Iske bina tumhara solution O(n^2) pe atka reh jaata hai, jabki interviewer O(n) expect kar raha hota hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Ek pointer ko array ke start pe rakho, doosre ko end pe.
2. Dono pointers ke values ka sum nikaalo aur target se compare karo.
3. Agar sum target se zyada hai, right pointer ko ek step peeche (left) le aao — kyunki bade number ko hatana hai.
4. Agar sum target se kam hai, left pointer ko ek step aage badhao — kyunki chhote number ko badhaana hai.
5. Agar sum target ke barabar hai, answer mil gaya.
6. Ye process tab tak chalao jab tak dono pointers mil na jaayen — har step mein search space ek se kam hota hai, isliye total kaam sirf array ki length jitna hota hai.

qa.q: When can two pointers replace a nested loop?
qa.a: When the array has structure (sorted, or a monotonic property) that lets you commit to moving one pointer without checking all remaining pairs. Two Sum: if the sum is too small, every pair with the left pointer is too small — so move left, no rescan needed.

qa.q: Why shrink the shorter side in Container With Most Water?
qa.a: The area is bounded by the shorter line. Moving the taller line inward can never increase area (height stays bounded by the shorter, width shrinks). Moving the shorter one is the only move that could improve — so that's the only one worth trying.

lessons.name: Sliding Window
lessons.desc: Maintain a contiguous window with two pointers that 'slide' across the array. For each element, either extend the window or shrink it to restore the invariant. Converts O(n²) substring scans into O(n).
lessons.q: What is the ONE question to ask before sliding window?
lessons.qsub: Why is each element visited at most twice? · How do you prove the O(n) bound? · What changes for a fixed-size window?
lessons.what:
String ya array mein sabse lamba (ya chhota) lagataar hissa dhoondhna hai jo ek shart poori kare. Naive tarika: har start aur end try karo — O(n²).

Par ek start se doosre start pe jaate waqt poora kaam dobara karne ki zaroorat hi nahi. Sirf itna dekho: kya naya aaya, aur kya purana gaya.

Yahi sliding window hai — ek chalta-firta range jise tum bada karte ho (right aage) aur chhota karte ho (left aage) taaki shart phir se poori ho jaaye. Right poore array mein ek baar chalta hai, left bhi ek baar — total O(n).
lessons.analogy: Socho ek WhatsApp group ke chat mein tumhe last 5 messages ka context dikhana hai jaise naya message aata hai — tum pura chat history dobara nahi padhte, bas sabse purana message list se hata dete ho aur naya jod dete ho, window hamesha 5 messages ki rehti hai.
lessons.why:
Ye pattern test karta hai ki tum redundant recomputation avoid kar sakte ho ya nahi. Fixed-size window (jaise 'har k size ka subarray') aur variable-size window (jaise 'sabse chhota subarray jiska sum >= target') dono interviewer ko ye dikhate hain ki tumhe pata hai O(n^2) se O(n) tak kaise jaana hai bina correctness todhe.

Kaise sochein:

1. Ek left aur ek right pointer dono ko array ke start pe rakho — window abhi khaali hai.
2. Right pointer ko aage badhao, naya element window mein add karo, aur window ki state update karo (sum, count, ya set).
3. Check karo ki window abhi bhi valid hai ya condition toot gayi.
4. Agar condition toot gayi ho (fixed-size mein size badh gayi, ya variable-size mein invariant fail ho gaya), left pointer ko aage badhao aur us element ko window se nikaalo, jab tak condition wapas theek na ho jaaye.
5. Har valid window pe answer (length, sum, ya count) update karte raho.
6. Right pointer ek hi baar poore array mein aage jaata hai aur left pointer bhi sirf aage jaata hai, kabhi peeche nahi — isliye total movement O(n) hota hai.

qa.q: What is the ONE question to ask before sliding window?
qa.a: What invariant must the window satisfy? For 'longest without repeating' it's 'no duplicate chars in window'; for 'minimum window with all chars' it's 'contains all needed chars'. Everything else — shrink logic and answer updates — follows mechanically from the invariant.

qa.q: When does sliding window NOT apply?
qa.a: When the answer can't be represented as a contiguous window — subsequences (order-preserving, skippable) need DP, and problems with negative weights may break the monotonic shrink property. If adding an element doesn't monotonicially violate the condition, the window can't slide.

lessons.name: Binary Search (minimize/maximize)
lessons.desc: The same halving idea applied to the space of answers, not just arrays: when feasibility is monotonic, binary search the answer value. Behind Koko, Split Array, and Capacity-to-Ship problems.
lessons.q: How do you recognize this pattern?
lessons.qsub: What if the answer range is huge (10^9)? · How do you pick lo for a 'maximize minimum' variant? · Why does the check have to be monotonic?
lessons.what:
"Minimum speed kya ho taaki saare kele ek din mein khatam ho jaayein?" Yahan koi sorted array hai hi nahi — par jawab ek range mein hai, maano 1 se 10 lakh.

Har value try karna slow hai. Par ek baat notice karo: chhoti speed kaam nahi karti, aur ek hadd ke baad har speed kaam karti hai. Ye monotonic hai — F F F F T T T T.

To binary search array ke index pe nahi, jawab ki value pe chalao. Har guess pe ek feasible(x) check karo (aksar O(n)), aur uske jawab se aadhi range phenk do. Total O(log R × n).
lessons.analogy: Socho tum ek almirah mein rakhe kapdon ke stack ke through search nahi kar rahe, balki tum guess kar rahe ho ki 'kitne rupaye mein ye TV milega' — dukaandaar ko bolte ho '5000 mein doge?', woh na bole to '7500?' poochte ho, matlab tum price ki range ko aadha karte jaate ho jab tak exact ya minimum acceptable price na mil jaaye — array nahi, sirf number line search ho raha hai.
lessons.why:
Ye ek bada mental shift hai jo interviewer specifically test karta hai — kya tum recognize kar sakte ho ki binary search sirf sorted arrays ke liye nahi, balki kisi bhi monotonic feasibility function ke liye applicable hai. Iske bina candidates linear search ya brute force try karte reh jaate hain aur time limit exceed karte hain, jabki ye pattern O(log(range) * check_cost) deta hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Answer ki possible minimum aur maximum value decide karo — ye tumhari search range banegi, array nahi.
2. Range ke beech ka value (mid) nikaalo aur ek 'feasibility check' function chalao — kya ye mid value se problem solve ho sakta hai.
3. Agar mid feasible hai aur tumhe minimum chahiye, to answer note karo aur range ko chhote half mein le jaao (kam value try karo).
4. Agar mid feasible nahi hai, to range ko bade half mein le jaao (zyada value try karo).
5. Maximize wale case mein logic ulta hota hai — feasible mile to zyada try karo, na mile to kam.
6. Range jab ek single point pe converge ho jaaye, wahi tumhara optimal answer hai.

qa.q: How do you recognize this pattern?
qa.a: The answer is a single number with a natural range (1..max), and checking 'does answer x work?' is easy but you'd otherwise have to test every value. The deciding feature: feasibility is MONOTONIC — once a value works, everything beyond it works too.

qa.q: Why while (lo < hi) instead of while (lo <= hi)?
qa.a: In answer-space search we converge to a single boundary index rather than find an exact hit, and there's always a valid answer in range. The l < r with hi = mid form converges cleanly without checking mid twice or risking an off-by-one on exact matches.

lessons.name: Prefix Sum
lessons.desc: Precompute prefix[i] = sum of the first i elements. Then any subarray sum [l, r) is prefix[r] - prefix[l] in O(1). The extension — prefix-sum counts in a hash map — solves 'subarray sum equals k'.
lessons.q: Why does prefix[0] = 0 help?
lessons.qsub: How does 2D prefix sum answer rectangle queries? · What does the Map[[0,1]] seed do? · How would you find the longest subarray with sum k?
lessons.what:
"Index 3 se 7 tak ka sum kya hai?" — aur ye sawaal baar-baar, alag-alag range ke liye aa raha hai. Har baar loop chalao to O(n) per query. 1000 query = bahut slow.

Ek baar mein prefix[i] bana lo — shuru se i tak ka running total. Ab kisi bhi range ka sum ek ghatav ban jaata hai: prefix[r] − prefix[l]. Ek baar ka O(n) kaam, phir har query O(1).

Aur asli power iske aage hai: prefix sums ko ek hash map mein rakh do. Ab "kitne subarray ka sum theek k hai" bhi ek hi pass mein — kyunki sum − k pehle dikha tha ya nahi, ye O(1) mein pata chal jaata hai.
lessons.analogy: Socho ek khaata (register) hai jismein har din ka 'total kharcha aaj tak' likha hota hai, na ki sirf us din ka kharcha. Agar tumhe 5 tarikh se 10 tarikh tak ka total kharcha jaanna hai, tum 10 tarikh ki running total se 4 tarikh ki running total ghata dete ho — har baar naya jodna nahi padta.
lessons.why:
Ye pattern test karta hai ki tum repeated range queries ko precompute se kaise fast bana sakte ho. Bina iske, range-sum ya subarray-sum-equals-k jaisi problems O(n^2) mein reh jaati hain. Prefix sum ke saath hash map jodna (prefix-sum-to-count) ek aur level test karta hai — kya tum cumulative state ko lookup-friendly structure mein convert kar sakte ho.

Kaise sochein:

1. Ek naya array banao jismein pehla element original array ke pehle element ke barabar ho.
2. Har agle index pe, pichla prefix value + current original value jodo — is tarah har position tak ka running total ban jaata hai.
3. Ab koi bhi range (i se j tak) ka sum nikalne ke liye, prefix[j] mein se prefix[i-1] ghatao.
4. Agar tumhe 'sum equals k' wale subarrays count karne hain, ek hash map banao jo har prefix sum ki frequency store kare.
5. Array ko ek baar traverse karte waqt, current prefix sum nikaalo aur check karo ki current_prefix - k hash map mein pehle kitni baar aaya hai — wahi count answer mein jodo.
6. Har step ke baad current prefix sum ko hash map mein bhi update karte jaao.

qa.q: Why does prefix[0] = 0 help?
qa.a: It makes range queries uniform — sum [l, r) is prefix[r] - prefix[l] without special-casing l = 0. Many off-by-one bugs disappear once you keep the zero-sentinel prefix.

qa.q: How does the hash-map trick count subarrays equal to k?
qa.a: A subarray [i, j] sums to k iff prefix[j] - prefix[i-1] = k, i.e. prefix[i-1] = prefix[j] - k. As you scan, every earlier running sum equal to current - k yields one valid subarray — a single O(1) map lookup per step.

lessons.name: Intervals
lessons.desc: Problems about ranges [start, end] — merging, inserting, counting overlaps. The near-universal trick is to SORT by start time, then compare each interval's start against the running end. Overlap test: next.start <= current.end.
lessons.q: What's the first move for almost every interval problem?
lessons.qsub: What's the difference between 'merge' and 'insert' strategies? · How does the greedy proof work for arrows/balloons? · When do you compare by start vs by end?
lessons.what:
Meetings ki list hai, har ek ka start aur end. Overlap dhoondhna hai, ya sabko merge karke ek saaf schedule banana hai.

Har interval ko har doosre se compare karo — O(n²). Par pehle sabko start time se sort kar do, aur poora khel badal jaata hai.

Sorted order mein koi interval apne turant agle se overlap kiye bina aur aage wale se overlap kar hi nahi sakta. Isliye sirf padosi check karna kaafi hai — ek pass, aur poora kharcha sirf sorting ka: O(n log n). Merge, insert, count — teeno isi ek trick pe khade hain.
lessons.analogy: Socho ek conference room ki booking sheet hai — agar tum saari bookings ko unke shuru hone ke time se sort kar do, to tumhe sirf ye check karna hai ki har agli booking pichli booking khatam hone se pehle to shuru nahi ho rahi — puri list ko baar baar cross-check karne ki zaroorat nahi padti.
lessons.why:
Interviewer ye dekhna chahta hai ki tumhe pata hai overlap detection O(n^2) nahi, O(n log n) (sorting ki wajah se) mein ho sakta hai — aur ye ki sorting se problem ka structure kaise simplify hota hai. Bina sort kiye, merge aur insert operations mein edge cases (partial overlap, containment, touching intervals) manage karna bahut messy ho jaata hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Saare intervals ko unke start value ke hisaab se sort kar do.
2. Ek 'result' list start karo aur usmein pehla interval daal do.
3. Baaki intervals ko ek ek karke dekho — current interval ko result ke last interval se compare karo.
4. Agar current interval ka start, last interval ke end se pehle ya barabar hai, matlab overlap hai — dono ko merge karo (end ko dono mein se bada wala rakho).
5. Agar overlap nahi hai, current interval ko result list mein ek naya entry ke roop mein jodo.
6. Jab tak saare intervals process nahi ho jaate ye chalte raho — result list ab final merged, non-overlapping intervals ki list hai.
where: O(n log n) · space: O(n) output

qa.q: What's the first move for almost every interval problem?
qa.a: Sort — by start for merging, by end for 'max non-overlapping'. Intervals have no inherent order, so sorting imposes the structure that makes a linear sweep meaningful.

qa.q: Why does sorting by end maximize the number of non-overlapping intervals?
qa.a: A greedy choice: taking the interval that ends earliest leaves the most room for the rest. This is the classic interval-scheduling proof — if any optimal solution differs, swapping in the earliest-ending interval never hurts.

lessons.name: Weekly Timed Mock (start here)
lessons.desc: From this phase onward: one 45-minute timed mock every week — 2 problems, no hints, talking out loud. Solving in your room and solving under a clock are different skills; start training the second one now, not in week 23.
lessons.q: Which problems go into a weekly mock?
lessons.qsub: Did I say the brute force and its complexity within the first 5 minutes? · Did I go silent for more than 30 seconds? · Did I test with an example before saying "done"?
lessons.what: Har hafte ek baar, 45 minute ka timer lagao, 2 problems uthao, aur bol-bol ke solve karo — jaise interviewer saamne baitha hai. Phone se screen + awaaz record karo.
lessons.why:
Google ka round knowledge se zyada performance test karta hai: ~20-25 minute mein Medium, saath mein soch ko bolna, edge cases khud pakadna. Ye aadat 4 hafte mein nahi banti — isliye Phase 3 (week 7) se shuru karo, taaki Phase 9 tak ~15 mocks ho chuke hon.

Kaise sochein:

0-5 min: problem dobara bolo, constraints aur examples clear karo.
5-10 min: brute force + complexity bolo, phir better approach.
10-30 min: code likho, bolte raho.
30-40 min: dry run, edge cases, complexity.
Baad mein recording dekho: kahan chup hue, kahan atke — ek aadat fix karo agle hafte ke liye.
where: 10-15 min after · space: log in P9 → Timed Mock template

qa.q: Which problems go into a weekly mock?
qa.a: One from the current phase and one from an older phase you have not touched in 2+ weeks. Pick problems you have NOT solved before when possible (use the LeetCode list for the same pattern). The old-phase problem doubles as spaced repetition.

qa.q: What if I fail the mock?
qa.a: That is the point — a failed mock in week 8 is cheap, a failed onsite is not. Write down WHERE you got stuck (understanding, approach, code, or bugs) and re-solve that exact problem 3 days later without looking.

lessons.name: Binary Tree Structure
lessons.desc: A hierarchical structure where each node has at most two children (left, right). Recursive by nature — every subtree is itself a binary tree, which is why recursion is the natural tool.
lessons.q: Why is recursion natural for trees?
lessons.qsub: What's a leaf node? A full vs complete vs perfect tree? · Why does height() return 0 for null? · How would you build a tree from an array representation?
lessons.what:
Har node ke paas zyada se zyada do bachche — left aur right. Bas itni si baat hai.

Par asli baat ye hai: har subtree khud ek poora tree hai. Kisi bhi node ko pakdo — uska left subtree apne aap mein ek valid binary tree hai. Structure khud ko dohrata hai.

Isiliye tree problems recursion se hoti hain. Tumhe poora tree nahi sochna — sirf teen cheezein: is node ka kya karna hai, left se kya jawab aayega, right se kya jawab aayega. Baaki recursion sambhal legi.
lessons.analogy: Company ka org chart. Tum apne do direct reports se poochte ho "tumhare neeche ka kya haal hai?" — unke neeche ke 200 logon ka hisaab wo khud sambhalte hain. Tumhe poori company nahi dekhni, sirf do log.
lessons.why:
Ye poore Phase 4 ki neev hai. Jo bandaa "is node ka kaam + do bachchon ka jawab" wali soch mein problem tod sakta hai, uske liye DFS, BFS, height, diameter — sab aasaan ho jaata hai.

Aur ek chhupa hua trap: binary tree aur BST alag cheezein hain. Binary tree mein values ka koi order nahi hota. "Tree" sun ke sorted maan lena sabse aam galti hai — pehle poochho.

Kaise sochein:

1. Har node ke teen hisse: apna value, left ka reference, right ka reference.
2. Bachcha nahi hai? Reference null — yahi tumhara base case hai.
3. root sabse upar wala node, jiska koi parent nahi. Ye kho gaya to poora tree kho gaya.
4. Har recursive function ka wahi dhaancha: if (!node) return <khaali jawab> → left ka jawab lo → right ka jawab lo → dono ko is node ke saath jodo.
5. "Khaali jawab" problem pe depend karta hai — count ke liye 0, sum ke liye 0, exists ke liye false, list ke liye [].
6. Space O(h) hai — stack pe ek waqt mein utne frames jitni tree ki height. Balanced pe O(log n), skewed pe O(n).

qa.q: Why is recursion natural for trees?
qa.a: A binary tree is defined recursively: a node plus two (possibly empty) binary trees. The recursive function mirrors the definition exactly — handle the empty case, trust the call for each child, combine results. Iteration needs a manual stack/queue instead.

qa.q: What's the space complexity of tree recursion?
qa.a: O(h), the height — the call stack holds one frame per level of the tree. Balanced: O(log n). Degenerate (every node has one child): O(n). An iterative traversal with an explicit stack has the same worst case but no native stack-overflow risk.

lessons.name: DFS (Preorder / Inorder / Postorder)
lessons.desc: Depth-first search visits a node and recurses down one whole subtree before the other. The three orders differ only in WHEN you process the node: before children (pre), between (in), after (post).
lessons.q: When do you use postorder?
lessons.qsub: How do you write DFS iteratively? · What's the difference between a 'path' and a 'subtree' in DFS? · Why does preorder + inorder uniquely reconstruct a binary tree?
lessons.what:
DFS ka matlab: ek subtree mein poora neeche tak jao, tabhi doosre pe aao. Ye ek hi raasta hai — teen "orders" alag traversal nahi hain.

Farak sirf ek baat ka hai: node ko chhuo kab? Bachchon mein jaane se pehle (preorder), left ke baad par right se pehle (inorder), ya dono ke baad (postorder).

Aur ye timing bekaar ki detail nahi hai — problem hi tay karti hai. Jawab bachchon pe depend karta hai (height, diameter)? Postorder. BST se sorted output chahiye? Inorder. Tree copy ya serialize karna hai? Preorder.
lessons.analogy:
Almirah mein dabbe, dabbon ke andar dabbe. Tum ek dabba kholte ho, uske pehle sub-dabbe mein poori tarah ghus jaate ho, tabhi wapas aa kar doosra kholte ho.
Note kab likhte ho — dabba kholte hi, beech mein, ya band karte waqt — yahi teen orders hain. Raasta wahi ka wahi.
lessons.why:
Interviewer ye nahi dekhta ki tum teen functions likh sakte ho. Wo dekhta hai ki tum sahi order chun sakte ho ya nahi.

Sabse zyada kaam ka insight: postorder tab chahiye jab node ka jawab uske bachchon ke jawab se banta ho. Height, diameter, "balanced hai kya", "is subtree ka sum" — sab postorder hain. Aur inorder BST ka "secret weapon" hai — sorted output muft mein.

Kaise sochein:

1. if (!node) return — hamesha pehli line.
2. Preorder: node ko process karo → left mein poora jao → right mein poora jao.
3. Inorder: left mein poora jao → node process karo → right mein jao.
4. Postorder: left → right → phir node process karo. Yahan node ke paas dono bachchon ke jawab already hain.
5. Raasta yaad rakhna hai (path problems)? Ek array neeche le kar jao, aur wapas aate waqt pop() kar do — yahi backtracking hai.
6. Time hamesha O(n) — har node ek baar. Space O(h) — stack.

qa.q: When do you use postorder?
qa.a: When the answer at a node depends on its children's answers — height, diameter, max path sum, balance checks. You must compute children first, which is exactly postorder. Preorder is for when you can decide at the node before descending.

qa.q: What is inorder traversal of a BST useful for?
qa.a: It visits nodes in sorted order. That powers Kth Smallest in a BST and validating a BST (check the sequence is strictly increasing).

lessons.name: BFS (Level Order)
lessons.desc: Breadth-first search visits level by level using a queue: process all nodes at depth d before any at depth d+1. The queue-size snapshot trick cleanly separates levels.
lessons.q: Why do you snapshot the queue size?
lessons.qsub: How do you find the tree's minimum depth with BFS early-exit? · What's the queue's worst-case width? · How would you detect if a tree is a perfect binary tree with BFS?
lessons.what:
Building ko manzil-dar-manzil dekho. Pehle ground floor ke saare kamre, phir first floor ke, phir second. Kisi ek kamre mein ghus ke sabse upar tak nahi bhaagna.

Recursion se ye nahi hoga — recursion ka swabhav hi ek direction mein neeche jaana hai. Isliye yahan queue chahiye: jo pehle aaya, wo pehle nikla.

Aur poore BFS ka ek hi trick hai: level shuru karne se pehle queue ka size naap lo. Utne hi nodes is level ke hain — jo iske baad add honge wo agle level ke hain. Ye ek line levels ko saaf-saaf alag kar deti hai.
lessons.analogy: Talaab mein patthar phenka. Lehrein ek-ek ring banake phailti hain — pehle 1 kadam ki doori wale sab, phir 2 kadam wale. Isiliye jo cheez pehli baar milti hai, wo sabse nazdeek hoti hai. Shortest path ka poora jawab isi ek baat mein hai.
lessons.why:
Do wajah. Pehli: level-wise jawab chahiye — "har level ka average", "right side view", "zigzag". Ye DFS se ho to jaata hai par bhaari padta hai.

Doosri, aur badi: shortest path. Minimum depth nikaalni hai? DFS poore gehre subtree mein bhatak sakta hai, jabki jawab bagal wale chhote branch mein tha. BFS pehli baar jahan pahunche, wahi sabse chhota hai — guarantee.

Kaise sochein:

1. Ek queue banao, usme root daal do. (Pehle !root check kar lo.)
2. Jab tak queue khaali na ho, loop chalao.
3. Loop ke shuru mein size = queue.length naap lo — ye is level ki ginti hai.
4. Theek size baar: front se node nikaalo, process karo, uske left aur right (jo maujood hon) peeche jod do.
5. Utne node nikal gaye = ek level poora. Agla iteration agla level.
6. JS mein shift() mat use karna — wo O(n) hai. Ek head index rakho aur badhate jao.

qa.q: Why do you snapshot the queue size?
qa.a: Without it, the inner loop would keep draining newly-enqueued children, merging levels together. The snapshot fixes how many nodes belong to the current level before you add any of the next level.

qa.q: BFS vs DFS on a tree — when do you choose BFS?
qa.a: BFS when the answer is level-based or you want shortest path (fewest edges). DFS when you need recursion's simplicity for path/sum computations. BFS typically uses more memory (queue width) than DFS (stack depth) on wide trees.

lessons.name: Binary Search Tree
lessons.desc: A binary tree with the ordering invariant: left subtree < node < right subtree. Searches halve the space each step — O(log n) on balanced trees. Inorder traversal yields sorted order.
lessons.q: How do you validate a BST without comparing to global min/max?
lessons.qsub: What makes a BST unbalanced, and what's the worst-case height? · How do you insert without breaking the invariant? · How would you find the lowest common ancestor in a BST (using values)?
lessons.what:
Binary tree mein values ka koi order nahi hota. BST mein ek niyam lag jaata hai: left subtree ki saari values node se chhoti, right subtree ki saari badi.

Bas is ek niyam se har comparison pe aadha tree khatam ho jaata hai. Binary search, par array ki jagah tree pe — O(h).

Aur ek bonus muft mein: inorder traversal se values sorted nikalti hain. Kyunki inorder ka matlab hi hai "pehle saare chhote, phir main, phir saare bade". Isliye BST ke aadhe sawaal (kth smallest, validate, range sum) inorder se hi hote hain.

Par yaad rakho: O(log n) tabhi jab tree balanced ho. Sorted data insert karoge to tree ek linked list ban jaayega — O(n).
lessons.analogy: Register jisme har page pe niyam hai: baayein wale hisse mein isse chhote naam, daayein mein isse bade. Naam dhoondhna hai? Poora register nahi padhna — har page pe bas ek faisla: baayein ya daayein. Par agar naam alphabet ke order mein hi daale gaye ho, to sab ek hi taraf lag jaate hain — aur register wapas ek lambi list ban jaata hai.
lessons.why:
BST validate karna interview ka classic trap hai. Log sirf parent se compare karte hain — aur ye galat hai. Node ko apne saare ancestors ki hadd maannī padti hai. Isliye (lo, hi) bounds neeche le jaani padti hain.

Doosra test: O(log n) bol dena aur balance ka zikr na karna. Skewed BST pe sab O(n) hai. Ye caveat khud bolna alag se points deta hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Search: root se shuru. Target chhota → left. Bada → right. Barabar → mil gaya.
2. Insert: wahi raasta chalo jab tak null na mile — wahin naya node.
3. Validate: har node ko (lo, hi) range do. Left mein jaate waqt hi = node.val, right mein jaate waqt lo = node.val. Sirf parent se compare karna galat hai.
4. Kth smallest: inorder chalao aur ginte jao — k-va element hi jawab.
5. Delete ke teen case: bachcha nahi → hata do. Ek bachcha → usse replace. Do bachche → inorder successor (right subtree ka sabse chhota) laao, phir usse hatao.
6. Sab kuch O(h) hai. Balanced → log n. Skewed → n.

qa.q: How do you validate a BST without comparing to global min/max?
qa.a: Pass the allowed range (lo, hi) down: the left child must be < node.val, the right > node.val. This catches the classic trap — a node can be within bounds of its parent yet violate an ancestor (e.g. a 15 in the right subtree of a 10).

qa.q: Why does inorder traversal give sorted order?
qa.a: By the BST invariant, everything in the left subtree is smaller than the node and everything on the right is larger. Visiting left → node → right therefore emits values in ascending order — that's the definition of sorted.

lessons.name: Construct Tree from Traversals
lessons.desc: Two traversals can uniquely rebuild a binary tree. Preorder + inorder: the first preorder value is the root; find it in inorder to split left/right subtrees. Recursion + an index map does the rest.
lessons.q: Why does preorder + inorder uniquely determine a tree?
lessons.qsub: How does the version with postorder differ? · What does the index map save you? · When does the recursion need the current root's position?
lessons.what:
Sirf do lists di hain — preorder aur inorder — aur poora tree wapas banana hai. Pehli nazar mein namumkin lagta hai: traversal mein to structure dikhta hi nahi.

Par ek baat pakki hai: preorder ka pehla value hamesha root hota hai. Ab us value ko inorder mein dhoondho. Uske baayein jo hai wo poora left subtree hai, daayein jo hai wo poora right subtree.

Bas — ab dono taraf yahi dohrao. Har baar preorder ka agla value naya root, aur inorder us root ke aaspaas do hisse mein bat jaata hai.

Ek aur baat: har baar inorder mein root ko dhoondhna O(n) hai — poora kaam O(n²). Ek hash map (value → index) bana lo, lookup O(1) ho jaata hai aur total O(n).
lessons.analogy: Ek kahani do tarah se sunayi gayi. Pehli version batati hai kis cheez se shuruaat hui (preorder ka pehla = root). Doosri version har cheez ko kram mein rakhti hai. Shuruaat wali cheez ko doosri list mein dhoondh lo — uske pehle ka sab "ek shakha", baad ka sab "doosri shakha".
lessons.why:
Ye teen cheezein ek saath test karta hai: recursion, hash map, aur index tracking. Naive solution mein log array slice karte rehte hain — wo O(n²) banata hai. Indices paas karna hi sahi jawab hai.

Aur ek conceptual sawaal jo aksar aata hai: preorder + postorder kaam kyun nahi karta? Jawab: unse pata hi nahi chalta ki ek akela bachcha left hai ya right. Inorder hi wo list hai jo left aur right ko alag karti hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Inorder ka ek hash map bana lo: value → index. Ye O(1) lookup dega.
2. Preorder pe ek pointer rakho jo sirf aage badhta hai — pre = 0.
3. Recursion ko inorder ki range do: build(lo, hi). lo > hi → null.
4. preorder[pre++] se naya node banao. Uska index inorder mein map se nikaalo — maano i.
5. Left pehle banao: build(lo, i-1). Phir right: build(i+1, hi). Order zaroori hai — preorder mein left ka poora hissa right se pehle aata hai.
6. Inorder + postorder ho? Root aakhri value hai, pointer peeche chalega, aur right pehle banana padega.

qa.q: Why does preorder + inorder uniquely determine a tree?
qa.a: Preorder's first element is the root. Inorder tells you exactly which nodes are in the left and right subtrees (everything before/after the root). Recursing with those split ranges reconstructs the whole tree — one root per preorder element, one split per inorder lookup.

qa.q: Why can't you reconstruct from preorder + postorder alone?
qa.a: Those two orders both describe the tree from the 'outside' — you can't always tell left from right children when a node has one child. Preorder + postorder determines a tree only up to mirror images.

lessons.name: Height, Depth, Diameter
lessons.desc: The measurement family: height (node → deepest leaf), depth (root → node), diameter (longest path between two nodes). Height uses postorder; diameter is 'left height + right height' computed along the way.
lessons.q: What's the difference between depth and height?
lessons.qsub: Is the diameter always through the root? · How do you count nodes instead of edges? · How would you return the actual diameter path, not just its length?
lessons.what:
Teen sawaal jo ek jaise lagte hain par alag hain:

Height — is node se neeche sabse door leaf tak kitna. Depth — root se is node tak kitna neeche. Height ka ulta. Diameter — poore tree mein kisi bhi do nodes ke beech ka sabse lamba raasta.

Height ke liye postorder chahiye — kyunki apni height jaanne se pehle dono bachchon ki height chahiye. Depth ke liye preorder — wo upar se neeche aati hai.

Diameter ka asli trick alag hai: raasta root se guzre ye zaroori nahi. Wo poora ek subtree ke andar bhi ho sakta hai. Isliye function height return karta hai par diameter alag se track hota hai — ek hi pass mein dono.
lessons.analogy: Family tree. Height = tumse neeche sabse door parpota kitni peedhi door hai. Depth = tum sabse purane purvaj se kitni peedhi neeche ho. Diameter = poore khandaan mein do rishtedaron ke beech ka sabse lamba rishta — aur wo do cousins ke beech bhi ho sakta hai, purvaj se guzre bina.
lessons.why:
Diameter ek classic interview trap hai. Naive solution: har node pe height dobara nikaalo — O(n²). Interviewer dekhta hai ki tum ek hi traversal mein height nikaalte-nikaalte diameter bhi track kar sakte ho.

Aur ye pattern aage bahut kaam aata hai: function jo return kare wo alag, aur jo track kare wo alag. Max Path Sum, Longest Univalue Path, Balanced check — sab isi shakal ke hain.

Kaise sochein:

1. Height: null → 0. Warna 1 + max(left, right). Postorder.
2. Depth: root se chalte waqt ek counter neeche le jao — depth + 1. Preorder.
3. Diameter: har node pe uske through jaane wala sabse lamba raasta = leftHeight + rightHeight.
4. Us value se ek bahar wala best update karo.
5. Par return karo 1 + max(left, right) — kyunki parent ke liye sirf ek taraf ka raasta kaam ka hai (raasta node pe mud nahi sakta).
6. Ye "return kuch, track kuch aur" wala pattern rat lo — poore Phase 4 mein baar-baar aayega.

qa.q: What's the difference between depth and height?
qa.a: Depth of a node: number of edges from the root down to it (root depth 0). Height of a node: number of edges from it down to its deepest leaf (leaf height 0, or 1 depending on convention — agree before coding). Depth is computed top-down, height bottom-up.

qa.q: Why does the diameter function return height but track diameter separately?
qa.a: The diameter at a node is left height + right height, but to let its PARENT compute a path, only the node's own height (1 + max child height) matters. So the function returns height and writes the diameter to a shared best as a side effect.

lessons.name: Iterative DFS
lessons.desc: The explicit-stack version of depth-first traversal. Useful when recursion depth might overflow, or when the interview asks you to avoid recursion. A stack (LIFO) mimics the call stack exactly.
lessons.q: How does iterative inorder keep the 'left first' order?
lessons.qsub: How do you do iterative postorder? · What's the space advantage of iterative traversal? · When is recursion still the better answer?
lessons.what:
Recursive DFS bhi ek stack use karta hai — bas wo chhupa hua hai. JS engine har function call ka frame call stack pe rakhta hai. Wahi tumhara traversal ka raasta yaad rakh raha hai.

Problem: wo stack chhota hai. JS mein ~10,000 frames ke baad RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. Skewed tree ya bahut gehra tree pe ye asli dikkat hai.

Iterative DFS wahi kaam apne stack se karta hai — ek normal array. Wo heap pe rehta hai, jo bahut bada hai. Traversal bilkul same, control tumhare haath mein.

Par dhyaan do: space dono mein O(h) hi hai. Iterative kam memory nahi leta — bas alag jagah se leta hai. Ye interview mein bolna zaroori hai.
lessons.analogy:
Waiter jo order yaad rakh ke khud kitchen bhaagta hai — wo recursion hai. Kaam chal jaata hai, par uski yaaddasht ki hadd hai.
Ab ek notebook rakh lo jisme pending orders likhe jaate hain, aur koi bhi upar wala order utha ke kaam kar de. Wahi kaam, par notebook jitni chahiye utni moti ho sakti hai.
lessons.why:
"Iteratively kar sakte ho?" — ye sabse aam follow-up hai. Aur ye sirf syntax ka sawaal nahi hai. Interviewer dekh raha hai ki tum samajhte ho recursion asal mein ek stack hi hai.

Preorder mein ek chhoti si baat hai jo poori samajh dikha deti hai: right ko pehle push karo, left ko baad mein. Kyunki stack LIFO hai — jo baad mein daala, wo pehle niklega. Ye ek line galat likhi to order palat jaata hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Preorder: stack mein root daalo. Loop: pop karo, process karo, phir right push karo, phir left. Left baad mein daala → pehle niklega. Bas.
2. Inorder: do hisse. Jab tak cur hai, use push karte hue left mein neeche jao. Phir pop karo, process karo, aur cur = cur.right.
3. Inorder mein cur = cur.right likhna mat bhoolna — warna wahi node baar-baar aayega.
4. Postorder (aasaan tarika): preorder ulta chalao — node → right → left — aur aakhir mein poora result reverse kar do.
5. Postorder (asli tarika): har node ke saath ek flag rakho — pehli baar dikha to dobara push karo (flag ke saath), doosri baar dikha to process karo.
6. Loop condition: while (stack.length). Inorder mein while (cur || stack.length) — dono chahiye.

qa.q: How does iterative inorder keep the 'left first' order?
qa.a: Push every node along the left spine first — the stack holds them root-to-leaf. Pop the deepest leftmost, visit it, then step to its right child and descend that node's left spine again. This exactly reproduces recursion's left→root→right rhythm.

qa.q: Why is iterative preorder just a stack?
qa.a: Preorder visits the node BEFORE children, so you can push children onto a stack and immediately pop the next one to visit. Pushing right before left makes the stack pop left first — no extra bookkeeping needed.

lessons.name: Balanced BSTs (AVL / Red-Black)
lessons.desc: A plain BST can degenerate into a linked list, making every op O(n). Balanced trees rebalance on insert/delete to keep height O(log n): AVL enforces a 1-height-difference invariant using rotations; Red-Black uses color rules to bound imbalance to a factor of 2.
lessons.q: Why not just use a plain BST and get O(log n)?
lessons.qsub: What invariant does an AVL tree maintain? · How many rotations does an AVL insert need at most? · Why does a balanced BST beat a sorted array for inserts? · Name two real data structures built on balanced trees.
lessons.what:
Plain BST mein 1, 2, 3, 4 isi order mein insert karo. Har naya number right child ban ke jud jaata hai. Tumhara "tree" asal mein ek seedhi linked list ban gaya.

Ab search, insert, delete — sab O(log n) ki jagah O(n). BST ka poora faayda khatam. Aur ye koi rare case nahi hai — sorted data insert karna bahut aam hai.

Balanced BST is problem ko har insert/delete ke baad theek karta hai: check karta hai ki tree ek taraf jhuk to nahi gaya, aur jhuk gaya to kuch nodes ko rotate karke height wapas O(log n) pe le aata hai.

AVL sakht hai — har node pe height ka farak ≤ 1. Red-Black dheela hai — rang ke niyam se height ko dugne se zyada nahi hone deta.
lessons.analogy: Almirah mein kapde sirf ek taraf lagte ja rahe hain, doosri taraf khaali. Almirah gir sakti hai. Ek smart system har naye kapde ke baad dekhta hai kitna jhukav aa gaya, aur zaroorat pade to kuch kapde doosri taraf shift kar deta hai. Rozana thoda extra kaam — par almirah kabhi girti nahi.
lessons.why:
Ye topic implement karne ke liye nahi hai — bolne ke liye hai. Interview mein AVL rotations poora likhwana durlabh hai.

Jo test hota hai wo ye: kya tum jaante ho ki "BST O(log n) hai" adhoora jawab hai? Sahi jawab: "balanced BST pe O(log n), plain BST worst case O(n)".

Aur ye system design se judta hai: Java ka TreeMap, C++ ka std::map, database indexes (B-tree, jo isi parivaar se hai) — sab isi guarantee pe chalte hain.

Kaise sochein:

1. Balance factor = left height − right height. AVL mein ye hamesha -1, 0, ya 1 hona chahiye.
2. Insert karo jaise normal BST mein. Phir wapas upar aate hue har node pe balance factor check karo.
3. Factor 2 ya -2 ho gaya? Rotate karo.
4. Chaar case: LL (ek right rotation), RR (ek left rotation), LR aur RL (do rotations — ye do log bhoolte hain).
5. Rotation BST property todta nahi — wo sirf shape badalta hai, order nahi. Inorder rotation ke baad bhi wahi rehta hai.
6. Red-Black alag raasta leta hai — nodes pe rang, aur rang ke niyam. Kam rotations, isliye insert/delete tez; height thodi zyada, isliye search thoda dheela.

qa.q: Why not just use a plain BST and get O(log n)?
qa.a: Inserting sorted data into an unbalanced BST makes a linear chain — every op becomes O(n). Balancing guarantees the height bound structurally, regardless of insertion order.

qa.q: AVL vs Red-Black: which do you pick and why?
qa.a: AVL for search-heavy workloads (tighter height, faster lookups). Red-Black for write-heavy workloads (fewer rotations on insert/delete). They trade search speed against rebalance frequency.

lessons.name: Graph Representation
lessons.desc: How you store edges decides how fast every operation is. Adjacency list: node → list of neighbors, O(V+E) space, the default. Adjacency matrix: V×V booleans, O(V²) space, O(1) edge lookup. Edgelist: array of [u, v, weight], compact for sorting.
lessons.q: Adjacency list vs matrix — how do you choose?
lessons.qsub: How do you store a directed acyclic graph? · When would an edge list beat an adjacency list? · What's the space of each representation for n=1000, e=10000?
lessons.what:
Graph problem mein sabse pehla kaam: edges ki list ko aisi shakal do jisse "is node ke padosi kaun hain?" turant pata chale.

Adjacency list — har node ke saamne uske asli padosiyon ki list. Space O(V + E). Ye 95% problems ka default jawab hai.

Adjacency matrix — V × V ka grid, har cell mein "edge hai ya nahi". Space O(V²) chahe graph khaali ho. Faayda: edge check O(1).

Edge list — sirf [u, v, weight] ka array. Kruskal ke liye sahi, kyunki wahan edges sort karni hoti hain.
lessons.analogy: List = phone ki contacts — sirf jo log actually hain, wahi save hain. Matrix = shaadi ka seating chart jisme har jodi ke liye ek khaana bana hua hai, chahe wo do log ek doosre ko jaante bhi na hon. Sparse graph pe matrix ka 99% hissa khaali padta hai.
lessons.why:
Interviewer ye pehle 2 minute mein dekh leta hai. Galat representation chuni to tumhara O(V + E) solution chupke se O(V²) ban jaata hai.

Aur ek bug hai jo sabse zyada hota hai: undirected graph mein reverse edge daalna bhool jaana. Code chalta hai, crash nahi hota — bas aadha graph gayab rehta hai aur jawab galat aata hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. Input aksar edge list hoti hai: [[0,1],[1,2],[0,3]].
2. Ek array of arrays banao: Array.from({length: n}, () => []). Array(n).fill([]) mat likhna — saari rows ek hi array ban jaayengi.
3. Har edge [u, v] pe: g[u].push(v). Graph undirected hai? To g[v].push(u) bhi — dono.
4. Weighted hai? Padosi ko jodi banao: g[u].push([v, w]).
5. Nodes 1 se shuru ho rahe hain? To array n + 1 ka banao, ya har jagah -1 karo. Ye off-by-one bahut kaatta hai.
6. Matrix tabhi jab graph dense ho (E ≈ V²) ya edge check baar-baar chahiye ho.

qa.q: Adjacency list vs matrix — how do you choose?
qa.a: List wins when the graph is sparse (most real graphs) — O(V+E) space and neighbor iteration is cheap. Matrix wins for DENSE graphs or when you need O(1) 'is there an edge between u and v' checks, at the cost of O(V²) space.

qa.q: What's the most common bug in the first 2 minutes of a graph problem?
qa.a: Missing the second push for undirected graphs (only adding u→v, never v→u). Also confusing 1-indexed input with 0-indexed arrays. Checking these two up front saves entire wrong solutions.

lessons.name: BFS on Graphs
lessons.desc: Queue-based level-by-level exploration. On unweighted graphs it finds the SHORTEST path in edges. The visited set (or distance array) is mandatory — unlike trees, graphs have cycles.
lessons.q: Why must you mark visited when ENQUEUEING, not when popping?
lessons.qsub: When is BFS the right choice over DFS? · What's the queue's worst-case memory? · How do you reconstruct the actual path, not just the length?
lessons.what:
Graph pe BFS wahi hai jo tree pe tha — queue, level by level. Par ek naya khatra hai: graph mein cycle hoti hai. Tree mein wapas peeche jaane ka raasta hi nahi tha.

Isliye visited set ab optional nahi, zaroori hai. Bina uske queue kabhi khaali hi nahi hogi.

Aur BFS ka asli tohfa: unweighted graph pe shortest path. Kyunki wo ek-ek ring karke phailta hai, jo node pehli baar milta hai wo sabse kam edges mein mila hai — guarantee. DFS ye nahi de sakta.

Ek baat jo bahut log galat karte hain: visited ka nishaan queue mein daalte waqt lagao, nikaalte waqt nahi. Warna ek node kai baar queue mein ghus jaayega.
lessons.analogy:
Talaab mein patthar. Lehrein ek-ek ring banake phailti hain — pehle 1 kadam wale sab, phir 2 kadam wale. Isliye jo cheez pehli baar chhuti hai, wo sabse nazdeek hai.
Aur agar tum nishaan na lagao ki kahan-kahan lehar pahunch chuki hai, to gol-gol ghoomti rahegi.
lessons.why:
Ek hi sawaal se poora topic test ho jaata hai: "visited ka nishaan enqueue pe lagate ho ya dequeue pe?"

Dequeue pe lagaoge to ek node kai baar queue mein aa jaayega — kaam O(V + E) se badh kar exponential tak jaa sakta hai. Jawab sahi aayega, par TLE.

Doosra test: shortest path ke liye DFS chuna? Wo galat hai — DFS ka pehla mila raasta sabse chhota hone ki koi guarantee nahi.

Kaise sochein:

1. Queue banao, source usme daalo, aur usi waqt visited mein bhi daal do.
2. Level-wise chahiye? Loop ke shuru mein size naap lo — wahi tree wala trick.
3. Front se node nikaalo, uske padosi dekho.
4. Har unvisited padosi: pehle visited mark karo, phir queue mein daalo. Ye order zaroori hai.
5. Distance chahiye? Ya to level counter rakho, ya dist[v] = dist[u] + 1 likhо.
6. Multi-source: shuru mein hi saare sources queue mein daal do. Phir sab ek saath phailte hain — Rotting Oranges, 01 Matrix isi se hote hain.

qa.q: Why must you mark visited when ENQUEUEING, not when popping?
qa.a: If you mark on pop, the same node can be enqueued by multiple parents before it's popped — duplicates flood the queue and you can even corrupt distance values. Marking at enqueue guarantees each node enters once.

qa.q: What is multi-source BFS and when do you use it?
qa.a: Seed the queue with ALL starting nodes at distance 0 (rotting oranges start as all rotten cells; 01-matrix starts as all zeroes). The wavefront expands uniformly from every source — the first time a cell is reached is its true minimum distance.

lessons.name: DFS on Graphs
lessons.desc: Recursive (or stack-based) exploration that dives deep before backtracking. Great for connectivity (components, islands), cycle detection, and path existence. The visited set prevents infinite loops on cycles.
lessons.q: How does DFS detect cycles in a directed graph?
lessons.qsub: Why does DFS use less memory than BFS on wide graphs? · How do you count the size of each connected component? · What's the difference between visited and on-stack in cycle detection?
lessons.what:
Maze mein ek raasta pakad ke poora andar tak jao. Dead-end aaya? Peeche palto aur doosra raasta lo. Yahi DFS hai.

Graph pe DFS tree wale se ek jagah alag hai: visited set zaroori hai, warna cycle mein recursion kabhi rukegi nahi.

Par asli baat aage hai. Directed graph mein cycle dhoondhne ke liye sirf "visited" kaafi nahi hai. Ek node dobara mila — iska matlab do cheezein ho sakti hain: ya to uska kaam poora ho chuka hai (theek hai), ya wo abhi tumhare raaste pe khada hai (cycle!).

Isliye teen rang chahiye: 0 = abhi chhua nahi, 1 = abhi stack pe hai, 2 = poora ho gaya. Rang 1 wale pe pahunch gaye = cycle.
lessons.analogy:
Maze mein chalte waqt do tarah ke nishaan lagao. Chalk — "main abhi is raaste pe hoon". Sticker — "ye raasta poora dekh liya, kuch nahi mila".
Chalk wale nishaan pe wapas pahunch gaye? Matlab tum gol ghoom kar apne hi raaste pe aa gaye — cycle. Sticker pe pahunche? Bas skip kar do.
lessons.why:
Ye Phase 5 ka sabse zyada test hone wala concept hai: directed cycle detection ke liye teen state chahiye, do nahi.

Log binary visited se cycle dhoondhne ki koshish karte hain aur DAG ko bhi "cycle hai" bata dete hain — kyunki ek node do alag raaston se mil sakta hai bina koi cycle bane.

Aur undirected mein kahani alag hai: wahan do rang kaafi hain, bas parent ko skip karna padta hai — warna har edge apne aap "cycle" lagegi.

Kaise sochein:

1. Har node ke liye ek state array — shuru mein sab 0.
2. DFS mein ghuste hi state[u] = 1 (stack pe hoon).
3. Har padosi v pe: state[v] === 1 → cycle mil gayi, return. state[v] === 2 → skip. 0 → usme recurse karo.
4. Saare padosi ho gaye → state[u] = 2 (poora ho gaya). Tabhi return.
5. Undirected mein: binary visited chalega, par recursion mein parent bhejo aur v === parent ho to skip karo.
6. Graph ke kai tukde ho sakte hain — isliye har node se DFS try karo, jo pehle se visited na ho.

qa.q: How does DFS detect cycles in a directed graph?
qa.a: Use three colors: unvisited, on-stack, done. If during DFS you hit a node that's still 'on-stack', you've found a back edge — that's a cycle. The on-stack marker matters because a finished node is NOT a cycle (that's just a shared subtree).

qa.q: BFS vs DFS on a graph — how do you decide?
qa.a: BFS for shortest path and anything level-based; DFS for connectivity, components, cycles, and when recursion gives cleaner code. Memory: BFS uses queue width O(V), DFS uses stack depth O(V) worst case — comparable on dense graphs.

lessons.name: Union-Find (Disjoint Set)
lessons.desc: A data structure for dynamic connectivity: 'are u and v in the same set?' and 'join u and v's sets'. With path compression and union by rank, both operations are nearly O(1) — inverse Ackermann. Perfect for components and cycle checks in undirected graphs.
lessons.q: How does path compression make find nearly O(1)?
lessons.qsub: Why union by rank, not just path compression? · How does union-find detect a cycle in an undirected graph? · What's the memory footprint vs an adjacency list?
lessons.what:
Ek hi sawaal baar-baar poocha jaa raha hai: "kya u aur v ek hi group mein hain?" Aur beech-beech mein do group jud bhi jaate hain.

Har baar BFS/DFS chalana O(V + E) hai — aur ye sawaal hazaar baar aa sakta hai.

Union-Find ka idea seedha hai: har group ka ek mukhiya (root) hota hai. find(x) batata hai x ka mukhiya kaun hai. Do nodes ka mukhiya same → ek hi group. union(u, v) do mukhiyaon ko jod deta hai.

Naive version O(n) tak slow ho sakta hai — chain ban jaati hai. Do chhoti optimizations (path compression + union by rank) isse practically O(1) bana deti hain.
lessons.analogy:
Har WhatsApp group ka ek admin hai. "Ye do log ek group mein hain?" — dono ka admin poochho, same hai to haan.
Do group merge karne hain? Ek admin ko doosre ke neeche laga do.
Path compression = har baar admin pooch ke, beech ke saare logon ko seedha admin ka number de do — agli baar kisi ko chain nahi chalni padegi.
lessons.why:
Interviewer do cheezein poochta hai. Pehli: dono optimization kyun chahiye? Sirf path compression se bhi chalta hai, par union by rank ke bina pehli baar lambi chain ban jaati hai.

Doosri, aur zyada kaam ki: undirected graph mein cycle detection. Edge jodne se pehle poochho — kya ye dono already ek group mein hain? Agar haan, to ye edge cycle banayegi. Kruskal ka poora MST isi ek line pe khada hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. parent[i] = i — shuruaat mein har node apna khud mukhiya.
2. find(x): jab tak parent[x] !== x, upar chalte jao.
3. Path compression: upar jaate waqt raaste ke har node ko seedha root se jod do. Ek line: parent[x] = find(parent[x]).
4. union(u, v): dono ke root nikaalo. Same hain? Kuch mat karo (aur ye cycle ka signal hai).
5. Union by rank: chhote ped ko bade ke neeche lagao — warna ped lamba hota jaayega.
6. Components ginne hain? Har successful union pe counter -1 karo. Shuru mein n the.

qa.q: How does path compression make find nearly O(1)?
qa.a: After find(x), we rewire x and every node on its path to point directly at the root. The tree flattens over time, so subsequent finds are single pointer hops. Combined with union by rank (attach shorter tree under taller), total is inverse-Ackermann — effectively constant.

qa.q: Union-Find vs BFS/DFS for connected components?
qa.a: Union-Find shines when connections are discovered incrementally or you need many 'are they connected' queries without re-traversing. BFS/DFS is simpler when you just need a one-time component count on a static graph. Both are O(V+E) class; UF adds near-O(1) point queries.

lessons.name: Grid Problems
lessons.desc: A 2D grid IS a graph — each cell is a node, adjacent cells are edges. Add a visited set and BFS/DFS to solve islands, rotting oranges, flood fill, and surrounded regions without building an explicit graph.
lessons.q: Why is sinking the cell in-place a valid visited set?
lessons.qsub: How do you find the largest island's area? · How does Surrounded Regions flip only boundary-connected cells? · How would you BFS multi-source from all boundary cells?
lessons.what:
Grid dikhta matrix jaisa hai, par asal mein wo ek graph hai. Har cell ek node, aur uske upar-neeche-baayein-daayein wale cells uske padosi.

Jaise hi ye baat samajh aati hai, "Number of Islands", "Rotting Oranges", "Flood Fill" — sab normal BFS/DFS ban jaate hain.

Ek faayda: adjacency list banani hi nahi padti. Padosi ek chhote se dirs array se khud ban jaate hain: [[1,0],[-1,0],[0,1],[0,-1]].

Aur ek chalak trick: visited ke liye alag set rakhne ki zaroorat nahi. Cell ko hi badal do (land ko water bana do) — O(1) extra space, aur code chhota.
lessons.analogy:
Building ka floor plan. Har kamra ek node. Darwaza sirf bagal wale kamron ke beech hai — diagonal wale kamre se seedha raasta nahi (jab tak problem ne bola na ho).
Aur kamra dekh liya? Uspe nishaan laga do — alag register rakhne ki zaroorat nahi.
lessons.why:
Interviewer ye dekhta hai ki tum grid ko graph ke roop mein pehchan sakte ho ya nahi. Jo bandaa alag se adjacency list banane lagta hai, wo abhi tak "grid ek implicit graph hai" wali baat pakad nahi paaya.

Aur ek bug jo har baar hota hai: bounds check. grid[nr][nc] padh liya bina ye dekhe ki nr, nc andar hain ya nahi — undefined pe crash. Bounds pehle, cell baad mein.

Kaise sochein:

1. m = grid.length, n = grid[0].length. Rectangular maano.
2. dirs = [[1,0],[-1,0],[0,1],[0,-1]] — 4 direction. Diagonal chahiye to 8 — problem se confirm karo.
3. Har cell pe loop chalao. Land mila aur abhi tak dekha nahi → wahin se DFS/BFS shuru karo aur counter +1.
4. Us DFS/BFS ke andar: cell ko turant mark karo (ya '0' bana do), phir chaaron padosi try karo.
5. Har padosi pe pehle bounds, phir visited, phir value check — isi order mein.
6. DFS chuno agar area/shape chahiye. BFS chuno agar doori/steps chahiye, ya grid bahut bada ho (recursion overflow se bachne ke liye).
where: O(m × n) · space: O(m × n) worst

qa.q: Why is sinking the cell in-place a valid visited set?
qa.a: Mutating grid[r][c] = '0' marks it visited without O(m×n) extra memory. As long as '0' was already not-a-cell-of-interest, the mutation can't confuse later logic — a classic memory win the interviewer will appreciate.

qa.q: BFS or DFS for islands?
qa.a: Both give O(m×n). DFS is shorter to write (recursion). BFS avoids recursion-depth limits on huge grids and is the natural fit when the problem asks for distance spreading (Rotting Oranges). Know both and justify by grid size.

lessons.name: Dijkstra's Algorithm
lessons.desc: Shortest path in a graph with NON-NEGATIVE weights. BFS with a priority queue: repeatedly extract the closest unvisited node and relax its edges. O((V + E) log V) with a min-heap.
lessons.q: Why does Dijkstra fail on negative edge weights?
lessons.qsub: How is Dijkstra like BFS? · When do you use a visited set in Dijkstra (and when not)? · What changes if you want the path itself?
lessons.what:
BFS shortest path deta hai — par sirf jab har edge ka weight barabar ho. Google Maps pe aisa nahi hota: koi road lambi par tez, koi chhoti par jam wali.

Dijkstra BFS ka wahi roop hai, bas queue ki jagah min-heap. Har baar wo node uthao jahan tak ab tak ka sabse sasta raasta mila hai.

Us node se nikalne wali har edge pe ek sawaal poochho: "iske through jaane se koi doosra node aur sasta pad raha hai?" Haan → uski distance update karo aur heap mein daal do. Isi ko relaxation kehte hain.

Ek shart: koi bhi weight negative nahi hona chahiye. Dijkstra maan leta hai ki jo node ek baar sabse sasta nikla, wo aage aur sasta nahi ho sakta — negative edge ye assumption tod deti hai.
lessons.analogy:
Metro map jisme har line ka apna kiraya hai. Tum hamesha wo station chunte ho jahan tak ab tak sabse sasta pahuncha ja sakta hai, wahan se aage ke sab connections dekhte ho, aur agar koi naya sasta raasta khulta hai to chart update kar dete ho.
Ab socho koi line paise deti ho (negative) — to "ye station final ho gaya" wali soch hi tut jaati hai.
lessons.why:
Ye weighted shortest path ka default jawab hai, aur interviewer turant "negative weights pe kyun fail karta hai?" poochta hai. Ye samajh ke bolna hi asli test hai.

Doosra: stale entries. Heap mein ek hi node kai baar aa sakta hai, alag-alag purani distances ke saath. Pop karte waqt check karo — agar heap ki distance dist[] se badi hai, to wo purani entry hai, skip karo. Ye check chhoot gaya to code slow aur kabhi-kabhi galat ho jaata hai.

Kaise sochein:

1. dist array banao, sab Infinity. dist[src] = 0.
2. Min-heap mein [0, src] daalo — distance pehle, taaki heap usi se sort kare.
3. Heap se sabse chhoti distance wala node u nikaalo.
4. Stale check: d > dist[u] hai? Wo purani entry hai — continue.
5. Relax: har padosi v pe — dist[u] + w < dist[v] hua to dist[v] update karo aur [dist[v], v] heap mein daalo.
6. Heap khaali → khatam. dist mein har node tak ka sabse sasta raasta. Time O((V + E) log V).
where: O((V + E) log V) · space: O(V + E)

qa.q: Why does Dijkstra fail on negative edge weights?
qa.a: It greedily finalizes the closest node assuming no later path can improve it. A negative edge can reopen that assumption — a finalized distance might shrink after being locked. Bellman-Ford handles negatives by relaxing all edges V-1 times.

qa.q: Why skip stale heap entries?
qa.a: A node can be pushed to the heap multiple times as better distances are found. When the stale copy (larger distance) is popped, relaxing from it would be wrong and wasteful. Skipping when d > dist[u] keeps the result correct with lazy deletion instead of tracking membership.

lessons.name: Topological Sort
lessons.desc: Order the nodes of a DIRECTED ACYCLIC GRAPH so every edge u→v has u before v. Kahn's algorithm (BFS on in-degrees) is the go-to: peel off zero-in-degree nodes repeatedly. Detects cycles when not all nodes get processed.
lessons.q: Why does a zero-in-degree node always start a valid order?
lessons.qsub: What's the DFS-based alternative to Kahn's algorithm? · How do you produce a lexicographically smallest valid order? · Why is topo sort only defined on DAGs?
lessons.what:
Courses hain, aur kuch ke prerequisites hain. Ek aisi order banani hai jisme koi course apne prerequisite se pehle na aaye.

Kahn's algorithm ka idea seedha hai: wo course pehle karo jiski koi dependency bachi hi nahi — yaani in-degree = 0.

Use kar liya? Ab uspe depend karne wale saare courses ka in-degree 1 kam ho jaata hai. Jiska 0 ho gaya, wo ab "unblocked" hai — queue mein daal do. Yahi chain chalti rehti hai.

Aur ek bonus: agar aakhir mein saare nodes order mein nahi aaye, to graph mein cycle hai — kyunki cycle ke andar har node kisi na kisi pe atka hua hai, kisi ka in-degree kabhi 0 hota hi nahi.
lessons.analogy:
Office mein tasks. Pehle wahi task uthao jiski koi dependency pending nahi hai. Wo poora hua — ab jo tasks uspe ruke the, unme se kuch unblock ho gaye.
Aur agar ek bhi task na mile jo shuru ho sake, to samajh lo kahin do tasks ek doosre ka intezaar kar rahe hain — deadlock. Wahi cycle hai.
lessons.why:
Topological sort do sawaal ek saath solve karta hai: order aur cycle detection. Course Schedule I sirf poochta hai "possible hai kya", II poora order maangta hai — code lagbhag same.

Aur ek galti jo bahut hoti hai: edge ki direction ulti bana dena. "[a, b] ka matlab b karne se pehle a karo" — isko dhyaan se padho. Direction ulti hui to order bhi ulta aayega, aur code crash nahi karega.

Kaise sochein:

1. Graph aur indeg array dono banao. Har edge u → v pe: g[u].push(v) aur indeg[v]++.
2. Jitne nodes ka indeg === 0 hai, sab queue mein daal do — ek nahi, saare.
3. Queue se node u nikaalo, use order mein daal do.
4. Uske har padosi v ka indeg[v]--. 0 ho gaya? Queue mein daal do.
5. Queue khaali. Ab check: order.length === n? Haan → valid order. Nahi → cycle hai.
6. Lexicographically chhota order chahiye? Queue ki jagah min-heap use karo.

qa.q: Why does a zero-in-degree node always start a valid order?
qa.a: A node with no incoming edges has no prerequisites — it can be scheduled immediately without violating any dependency. Removing it only DECREASES other nodes' in-degrees, which is exactly 'satisfy one prerequisite'. Repeat until everything's scheduled.

qa.q: How does topological sort detect cycles?
qa.a: In a DAG, every step finds at least one zero-in-degree node. If the algorithm gets stuck with nodes remaining, all leftover nodes are in a cycle — none can ever drop to zero in-degree. So order.length < V means a cycle.

lessons.name: Minimum Spanning Tree (Prim / Kruskal)
lessons.desc: The MST connects every vertex with the minimum total edge weight. Kruskal sorts all edges and greedily adds them via union-find (O(E log E)). Prim grows one tree from a start vertex, always taking the cheapest frontier edge (O(E log V) with a heap).
lessons.q: When should you use Kruskal over Prim?
lessons.qsub: State the cut property in one sentence. · Why does Kruskal need the graph to be undirected? · How would you build the MST of a complete graph from (x,y) points? · What if the graph is not connected — what does Kruskal return?
lessons.what:
Nayi society mein har ghar tak bijli ki cable pahunchani hai. Cable mehengi hai — kam se kam total lambai mein saare ghar jud jaane chahiye, aur koi ghar chhoote nahi.

Jawab hamesha ek tree hota hai: n nodes ko jodne ke liye theek n - 1 edges chahiye. Ek bhi zyada matlab cycle, aur cycle ka matlab ek edge bekaar hai.

Kruskal: saari edges weight se sort karo. Sabse sasti se shuru karke uthate jao — par jo edge cycle banaye use chhod do. Cycle check Union-Find karta hai.

Prim: ek node se shuru karo. Har baar apne set se bahar jaane wali sabse sasti edge uthao. Ped ugta jaata hai. Min-heap se hota hai.
lessons.analogy:
Kruskal = property dealer. Saare available roads ko rate ke hisaab se list karta hai, sabse sasta pehle leta hai — bas dhyaan rakhta hai ki jo ilaaka already juda hua hai usko dobara na jode.
Prim = ek ped. Ek jagah se jad jamati hai aur hamesha apni sabse nazdeek (sasti) shakha ki taraf failti hai.
lessons.why:
MST aur Dijkstra sabse zyada confuse kiye jaane wale do algorithms hain — dono greedy hain, dono heap use karte hain, dono "minimum" bolte hain.

Par kaam bilkul alag hai. MST: sabko jodne ka total kharcha kam. Dijkstra: ek node se baaki tak ka har raasta chhota. MST ke andar ka raasta do nodes ke beech shortest ho, ye zaroori nahi.

Aur ek practical baat: graph connected hi na ho to MST banta hi nahi. Isliye aakhir mein check karo ki n - 1 edges use hui ya nahi.

Kaise sochein:

1. Kruskal: saari edges [u, v, w] ko w se sort karo.
2. Ek DSU banao. Har edge pe union(u, v) try karo. true aaya → edge le lo. false → cycle thi, chhod do.
3. n - 1 edges ho gayein → MST poora, ruk jao.
4. Prim: koi bhi node se shuru. Uski saari edges heap mein daal do.
5. Heap se sabse sasti edge nikaalo. Uska doosra sira already set mein hai? Skip. Nahi? Le lo, aur us naye node ki saari edges heap mein daal do.
6. Kaunsa chuno: edge list di hai ya graph sparse hai → Kruskal. Adjacency list hai ya graph dense hai → Prim.

qa.q: When should you use Kruskal over Prim?
qa.a: Kruskal when the edge list is already available (easy to sort) or the graph is sparse. Prim when you have adjacency and dense graphs — no global sort needed, just a heap of frontier edges.

qa.q: How do you detect a cycle in Kruskal?
qa.a: Union-find: if the two endpoints of an edge are already in the same component, adding it creates a cycle, so skip it. Path-compressed union-find makes this nearly O(1) per check.

lessons.name: Bellman-Ford (negative weights)
lessons.desc: Single-source shortest paths that also handle negative edge weights, unlike Dijkstra. Relax every edge V-1 times: each pass extends valid distances by one more edge. A V-th pass that still improves anything proves a negative cycle exists.
lessons.q: Why does Bellman-Ford need exactly V-1 passes?
lessons.qsub: When is Dijkstra wrong but Bellman-Ford right? · What does "relax an edge" mean? · Why is Bellman-Ford slower than Dijkstra? · How would you enforce a max of K edges (hops)?
lessons.what:
Dijkstra ek baat maan kar chalta hai: jo node ek baar sabse sasta nikal aaya, uski distance final hai. Negative edge ye baat tod deti hai — baad mein koi raasta usse aur sasta bana sakta hai.

Bellman-Ford koi assumption nahi karta. Wo saari edges ko bar-bar relax karta hai — theek V - 1 baar.

V - 1 kyun? Kyunki kisi bhi shortest path mein zyada se zyada V - 1 edges ho sakti hain (usse zyada matlab koi node dobara aaya, matlab cycle, jo shortest path mein hoti nahi). Har round khabar ko ek edge aur door tak pahunchata hai.

Aur ek muft ka tohfa: V-va round chalao. Ab bhi kuch ghat raha hai? Matlab graph mein negative cycle hai — jahan ghoom-ghoom kar distance hamesha kam hoti rahegi, aur shortest path define hi nahi hota.
lessons.analogy:
Shehar mein khabar phailna. Pehle round mein sirf source ke seedhe padosiyon tak pahunchti hai. Doosre round mein unke padosiyon tak. V-1 round mein sabse door wale tak bhi taazi khabar pahunch jaati hai.
Ab agar ek round aur chalao aur khabar phir bhi badal rahi hai — matlab kahin ek afwaah ka chakkar hai jo khud ko badalta rehta hai.
lessons.why:
Interviewer ka pehla sawaal: "Dijkstra kyun nahi?" Jawab: negative weights. Aur ye sirf theory nahi — currency arbitrage aur kuch routing protocols mein negative weights asli cheez hain.

Par interview mein iska sabse aam roop alag hai: Cheapest Flights Within K Stops. Wahan negative weights hain hi nahi — par "zyada se zyada k stops" wali shart hai. Dijkstra ye seedha handle nahi karta, par Bellman-Ford ke k+1 rounds bilkul yahi cheez hain.

Kaise sochein:

1. dist array, sab Infinity. dist[src] = 0.
2. V - 1 baar loop chalao.
3. Har round mein saari edges pe jao: dist[u] + w < dist[v] hua to dist[v] update karo.
4. Ek round mein kuch bhi nahi badla? Aage sab same rahega — wahin ruk jao (early exit).
5. Negative cycle: V-va round aur chalao. Ab bhi kuch ghata → negative cycle hai.
6. K-hop version: V-1 ki jagah k+1 rounds chalao, aur har round mein dist ki copy use karo — warna ek hi round mein khabar do edges aage nikal jaayegi.

qa.q: Why does Bellman-Ford need exactly V-1 passes?
qa.a: The shortest path in a graph with V vertices uses at most V-1 edges (simple path). Each pass extends distances by one more edge, so after V-1 passes every reachable shortest path is computed.

qa.q: How do you detect a negative cycle?
qa.a: Run one extra pass. If any edge can still relax a distance, a reachable negative cycle exists and shortest paths are undefined (they decrease forever).

lessons.name: Floyd-Warshall (all pairs)
lessons.desc: Computes shortest paths between every pair of vertices using dynamic programming. For each intermediate vertex k, check if routing through k improves any (i, j) distance. Simple, dense (O(V^3)), and works with negative edges (as long as no negative cycles).
lessons.q: Why must k be the outermost loop?
lessons.qsub: What does dist[i][j] mean after processing intermediate k? · How do you reconstruct the actual path after the distances? · Can Floyd-Warshall handle negative weights? · How do you detect a negative cycle with it?
lessons.what:
Ab tak har algorithm ek source se chalta tha. Yahan sawaal alag hai: har city se har city tak ka shortest distance ek saath chahiye.

Har node se Dijkstra chalana ek option hai. Floyd-Warshall doosra — aur uska idea itna simple hai ki poora code 4 line ka hai.

Ek-ek karke har node k ko "beech ka stop" maano, aur har jodi (i, j) se poochho: k se ho kar jaana seedha jaane se sasta hai kya? Haan to chart update kar do.

Yahi DP hai. k-va round ke baad matrix ka matlab hota hai: "0..k tak ke nodes ko beech mein use karke i se j ka sabse sasta raasta". Isiliye k ka loop sabse bahar hona chahiye — wo DP ki layer hai.
lessons.analogy:
Airline ka fare chart. Ek-ek karke har city ko hub maan kar poora chart dekho — "Dubai se ho kar jaana seedhi flight se sasta padta hai kya?" Har hub ke baad chart thoda aur sudhar jaata hai.
Saare hubs dekh liye — chart ab poora sahi hai.
lessons.why:
Do cheezein test hoti hain. Pehli: k sabse bahar kyun? Loop order badal diya to jawab chup-chaap galat aata hai, aur bug pakadna bahut mushkil hai.

Doosri: kab ye Dijkstra se behtar hai? Jawab: jab V chhota ho (~400 tak) aur saare pairs ka jawab chahiye. V bada hua to O(V³) bilkul nahi chalega — V = 1000 pe hi 100 crore steps.

Kaise sochein:

1. V × V matrix banao, sab Infinity.
2. dist[i][i] = 0 — khud tak ka kharcha zero. Ye seed bhoolna nahi.
3. Har edge [u, v, w] ke liye dist[u][v] = w. (Multi-edge ho to min lo.)
4. Teen nested loop: k bahar, phir i, phir j.
5. Andar bas ek line: dist[i][j] = min(dist[i][j], dist[i][k] + dist[k][j]).
6. Negative cycle: aakhir mein koi dist[i][i] < 0 hai? Matlab i se nikal kar wapas i pe aane mein faayda ho raha hai — negative cycle.

qa.q: Why must k be the outermost loop?
qa.a: Pass k assumes paths using intermediates 0..k-1 are final. If i or j were outermost, an improvement from pass k could be missed because the sub-results were not yet computed.

qa.q: When is Floyd-Warshall a better answer than Dijkstra from each node?
qa.a: For dense graphs and when V is small: running Dijkstra V times is O(V E log V), which is worse than O(V^3) when E is near V^2. Floyd-Warshall is also far simpler to write.

lessons.name: Euler Path / Hierholzer
